Log-returns are identified to contain a jump when their absolute value exceeds this threshold. The volatility estimate is then updated using only the log-returns not containing jumps, and a second-round threshold is determined. The procedure is repeated recursively until no further jumps are detected. Before application to empirical data, the reliability of the jump detection procedure was tested on simulated asset prices generated by a semi-martingale in which stochastic volatility shows a diurnal eƯect and leverage, and jumps occur at times generated by a Hawkes process and have Gaussian sizes.

title: A Tax Penalty as a Punishment? Legal Aspects of the Concurrence of Tax and Criminal Sanctions
affiliations: Masaryk University - Faculty of Law and Masaryk University - Faculty of Law

detail.title: A Tax Penalty as a Punishment? Legal Aspects of the Concurrence of Tax and Criminal Sanctions
detail.abstract: Tax crime in the Czech Republic has become increasingly important in recent years. This article focuses on an unintended consequence of tax crime, namely the issue of double jeopardy. In the Czech legal system, tax proceedings and criminal proceedings are conducted separately. The aim of this article is to determine whether it is possible to impose a tax penalty and a penalty in criminal proceedings at the same time without violating the ne bis in idem principle. The hypothesis assumes that the concurrence of these sanctions is possible if the penalty is not considered as a punishment in the sense of criminal law. For these purposes, the legal framework that defines tax and criminal proceedings in the Czech Republic is first analysed. Subsequently, the conditions under which it is possible to conduct these proceedings in the same case are identified, using an analysis of the case law of European and domestic courts. The authors conclude that tax penalties are punitive in nature and therefore the sanctions imposed must be considered. However, the current legal framework in the Czech Republic makes this very difficult, as the tax administrator is not granted discretionary powers when imposing penalties. Therefore, the following solutions are proposed: 1) change the legislation and allow discretion in imposing penalties, 2) do not impose penalties at all if a punishment has already been imposed in criminal proceedings, 3) merge the two proceedings and impose one sanction.

title: Sexualised Corruption in High-Income Democracies: Sub-National Evidence from the European Union
affiliations: Dublin City University - School of Law and Government and Dublin City University Business School

detail.title: Sexualised Corruption in High-Income Democracies: Sub-National Evidence from the European Union
detail.abstract: This article examines whether sexualised corruption – the abuse of public power to obtain sexual favours – emerges under the same opportunity structures as petty corruption in advanced democracies. Drawing on representative data from 40,663 respondents from the 2023 Global Corruption Barometer–European Union, we construct regionally disaggregated measures of sexualised corruption across all 27 member states. Our analysis shows that regional prevalence of petty corruption predicts sexualised corruption, but the relationship is conditional: it is strongest in affluent regions and in countries with lower overall corruption and greater gender equality, while in poorer or more corrupt settings sexualised corruption is elevated regardless of petty corruption levels. By contrast, petty corruption does not predict perceptions, which are concentrated in urban and educated regions even as experiences cluster in deprived areas. These findings indicate that rising corruption can inflict severe harms on women, even in countries relatively advanced in combating corruption and promoting gender equality.

title: Common Vs. Cross Ownership: Incentives to Divest Shareholding Interlocks
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Korea University and Humboldt University of Berlin - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Common Vs. Cross Ownership: Incentives to Divest Shareholding Interlocks
detail.abstract: We compare the stability of shareholding interlocks under common and cross ownership in a Cournot duopoly. While cross ownership tends to lead to its own demise due to firms' incentive to divest all shares they hold in rival firms, we demonstrate that common ownership exhibits enhanced stability. Specifically, no divestment occurs if interlocking shareholdings are large. Conversely, complete divestment occurs only if these shareholdings are relatively small, and partial divestment occurs if they fall within an intermediate range. This stability property is reinforced by the additional advantages of diversification and of maintaining toeholds in rival firms.

title: Delegation of Approval Authority in State-owned Share Transfers and Corporate Investment Decisions
affiliations: Sichuan University, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics and Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU)

detail.title: Delegation of Approval Authority in State-owned Share Transfers and Corporate Investment Decisions
detail.abstract: Government approval is central to state-owned share transfers, for which conflicts of interest and information frictions in the approval process may constrain reform outcomes. This study examines how delegating government approval authority affects the efficiency of stateowned share transfers. We exploit a 2018 policy reform (State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commissions Order No. 36) in China that permitted the delegation of approval authority for state-owned share transfers to state-owned entities or prefecture-level SASACs under specified conditions. We find that delegation significantly increases the likelihood of non-state and specialized investors acquiring state-owned shares. With changes of transferees, delegation improves investment sensitivity to profitability, particularly when approval is delegated to entities with stronger corporate governance or to regions with more developed institutional environments, highlighting that the effectiveness of delegation depends on the capacity of the delegated decisionmakers. Mechanism tests indicate that new shareholders enhance value orientation and provide firm-specific information. Additional analyses reveal that delegation enhances investment responsiveness to the idiosyncratic component of firm profitability. Our findings underscore the importance of approval rights allocation in shaping the ownership transfers and highlight how targeted delegation can improve the efficiency of state-owned enterprises.

reference: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-114
title: Earnings Instability
affiliations: University of Chicago, University of Chicago Booth School of Business, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and University of Chicago

detail.title: Earnings Instability

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-114
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper uses high-frequency administrative data to show that the majority of U.S. workers experience substantial month-to-month fluctuations in pay, even within ongoing employment relationships. This earnings instability is pervasive, but it has been masked in past analysis of annual data. Moreover, this instability is unequally distributed: lower-income, hourly workers face more instability than higher-income, salaried workers. This is because earnings instability arises in large part from firm-driven fluctuations in hours. This earnings instability is a meaningful source of economic risk: we provide causal evidence that it increases consumption volatility and also leads to greater job separations, and we find that workers have a high willingness to pay to reduce earnings instability. These findings suggest that short-term earnings risk is a significant and previously underappreciated feature of the labor market. * We thank Fiona Greig for the initial conversations which inspired this paper. We thank Niels Gormsen, Si.

title: Simple Incentives and Diverse Beliefs
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology - School of Economics

detail.title: Simple Incentives and Diverse Beliefs
detail.abstract: This paper studies a moral hazard problem in which the principal does not know the agent’s beliefs about the output generating process. The agent is risk neutral, transfers are subject to limited liability, and the principal evaluates contracts according to their worst-case payoff against a rich set of plausible agent beliefs. With common knowledge of the relationship between effort and expected output, optimal contracts are of the form $w(y) = \max (\alpha y + \beta , 0 )$. With or without common knowledge of that relationship, there are broad conditions under which optimal contracts are of the form $w(y) = \alpha y + \beta$ and the principal can not improve her payoff guarantee by screening, randomizing over contracts, or trying to learn the agent’s beliefs.

title: A Unified Framework for Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF): Reconciling Methodological Inconsistencies in Valuation Practice
affiliations: and DBS Global University

detail.title: A Unified Framework for Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF): Reconciling Methodological Inconsistencies in Valuation Practice

declarations.ethicsApproval: This research did not involve human or animal subjects and no ethical approval is required.

detail.abstract: The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) valuation method relies critically on the accurate calculation of Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF). Practitioners and academics currently utilize four primary formulas based on starting points from the income and cash flow statements: EBIT, Net Income, Cash from Operations, and EBITDA. This paper identifies a critical flaw: these standard formulas often yield different FCFF values from the same dataset, undermining DCF valuations and leading to material errors in investment decisions, mergers and acquisitions, and corporate strategy. We demonstrate that this inconsistency stems from the differential treatment of non-operating items and tax shields on depreciation. This paper proposes a unified framework that systematically adjusts for these items, ensuring all four calculation paths converge on a single, consistent FCFF value. This enhancement provides analysts with a robust, error-resistant framework for valuation, model auditing, and reducing arbitrariness in financial analysis.

title: The Folk Theorem with Endogenous Discounting and Unobserved Mixtures
affiliations: University of Rochester and University of Colorado Boulder

detail.title: The Folk Theorem with Endogenous Discounting and Unobserved Mixtures

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study infinitely repeated games in which the players’ rates of time preference may evolve endogenously in the course of the game. Our goal is to strengthen the folk theorem of Kochov and Song (2023) by relaxing the assumption of observable mixtures. To that end, we identify and impose a new sufficient condition on preferences. The condition holds automatically in the standard case of time-separable utilities and a common discount factor, while being generic in ours.

title: Can The EU Levy Its Own Taxes? A “Corporate Resource for Europe” (Re)enters A Legal Minefield
affiliations: International Bureau of Fiscal Documentation (IBFD)

detail.title: Can The EU Levy Its Own Taxes? A “Corporate Resource for Europe” (Re)enters A Legal Minefield
detail.abstract: This blog post examines the newly proposed Corporate Resource for Europe ('CORE'), and its potential consequences for the future EU financing from the constitutional and EU law perspective. It explicitly interrogates the question of the legal basis and whether the definition of the contribution as a tax or not a tax changes the legal consequences of its introduction.

title: Private vs Public Credit Markets: Introducing the Credit Adaptation Efficiency Index (CAE) for Measuring Structural Responsiveness in Capital Allocation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Private vs Public Credit Markets: Introducing the Credit Adaptation Efficiency Index (CAE) for Measuring Structural Responsiveness in Capital Allocation
detail.abstract: We introduce the Credit Adaptation Efficiency (CAE) Index, a novel metric for evaluating how effectively credit markets adapt capital allocation in response to changing risk conditions and borrower quality. The CAE framework is applied to compare private versus public credit markets, using aggregated data from reputable sources (Federal Reserve, BIS, IMF, OECD, S&P LCD, PitchBook, World Bank) to examine three recent stress events: the COVID-19 credit freeze of early 2020, the 2022 interest rate hike cycle, and the 2023 commercial real estate (CRE) stress. We formally define CAE with a mathematical model that relates changes in credit supply to shifts in risk perception, borrower quality, and liquidity conditions. Our results show distinct differences in adaptive behavior: private credit often exhibits a more resilient credit supply during market disruptions, whereas public credit allocation is more sensitive to immediate risk re-pricing. We estimate CAE values for public and private credit in each case study, highlighting instances where private lenders maintained or quickly resumed lending amid rising risk premiums (e.g. during the 2022 tightening, private direct lending AUM grew even as leveraged loan and high-yield bond markets stagnated). The paper discusses implications for institutional investors (e.g. dynamic allocation decisions between public and private debt), for regulators (monitoring systemic resilience via CAE trends), and for market participants (designing strategies to enhance adaptability). We conclude that the CAE Index fills a crucial gap in existing metrics by quantifying structural responsiveness in capital allocation, offering a practical tool to assess market efficiency under stress.

title: Smart Power Limits: Designing Shortage Mechanisms for Extreme Events
affiliations: Northwestern University - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Smart Power Limits: Designing Shortage Mechanisms for Extreme Events

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
As shortages of resources like water and electricity due to extreme weather events become more frequent, high prices alone may fail to curb demand, making shortages more common. We examine a power limit policy for residential electricity households that rations electricity consumption rather than setting it to zero, as in a traditional rolling blackout. We find that power limits can provide equivalent savings to large blackouts, even when generous. Additionally, due to selection, power limits reduce the number of households affected by a shortage event. We conclude by discussing the welfare consequences of power limits and their heterogeneous impact across households.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Earnings Responses to Social Security Contributions: Evidence from Older Workers in Canada
affiliations: McMaster University and

detail.title: Earnings Responses to Social Security Contributions: Evidence from Older Workers in Canada

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper documents sharp bunching in third-party reported employment earnings at a basic exemption for social security contributions among older workers. Beginning in 2012, workers age 60-64 who were receiving a public pension were required to make social security contributions equal to 9.9 percent of their employment earnings above a basic exemption threshold of $3,500. Using administrative data on third-party reported earnings and a differences-in- bunching estimator we document sharp bunching at the $3,500 threshold. We argue that our results represent new evidence on the role of firms in mediating the earnings response to payroll taxes.

title: The Sticky Leverage Channel of Monetary Policy: Evidence from Dollar-Denominated Debt in Latin America
affiliations: Virginia Tech - Department of Economics, University of International Business and Economics (UIBE) - School of Banking and Finance and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Sticky Leverage Channel of Monetary Policy: Evidence from Dollar-Denominated Debt in Latin America
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the sticky leverage channel of monetary policy transmission. When debt obligations have fixed nominal value in foreign currency, a foreign monetary expansion reduces the burden of existing debt measured in local currency and boosts firm performance. Using data on Mexican and Brazilian publicly listed firms with substantial dollar-denominated debt, we show that firms with higher dollar leverage experience greater increases in equity value, capital expenditure, and sales following a U.S. monetary expansion. These effects are more pronounced for firms with longer debt maturities or larger net export positions.

title: Artificial Writing and Automated Detection
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Artificial Writing and Automated Detection
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly used for written deliverables. This has created demand for distinguishing human-generated text from AI-generated text at scale, e.g., ensuring assignments were completed by students,  product reviews written by actual customers, etc. A decision-maker aiming to implement a detector in practice must consider two key statistics:  the False Negative Rate (FNR), which corresponds to the proportion of AI-generated text that is falsely classified as human, and the False Positive Rate (FPR), which corresponds to the proportion of human-written text that is falsely classified as AI-generated. We evaluate three leading commercial detectors---Pangram, OriginalityAI, GPTZero---and an open-source one ---RoBERTa---on their performance in minimizing these statistics using a large corpus spanning genres, lengths, and models. Commercial detectors outperform open-source, with Pangram achieving near-zero  FNR and FPR rates that remain robust across models, threshold rules, ultra-short passages, "stubs" (≤ 50 words) and 'humanizer' tools. A decision-maker may weight one type of error (Type I vs. Type II) as more important than the other. To account for such a preference, we introduce a framework where the decision-maker sets a policy cap---a detector-independent metric reflecting tolerance for false positives or negatives. We show that Pangram is the only tool to satisfy a strict cap (FPR ≤ 0.005) without sacrificing accuracy. This framework is especially relevant given the uncertainty surrounding how AI may be used at different stages of writing, where certain uses may be encouraged (e.g., grammar correction) but may be difficult to separate from other uses.

title: Performance Evaluation Relative to a Predecessor: CEO Turnover and Pre-Appointment Firm Performance
affiliations: University of Miami - Department of Accounting, University of Miami - Department of Accounting, The Chinese University of Hong Kong and University of Technology Sydney (UTS)

detail.title: Performance Evaluation Relative to a Predecessor: CEO Turnover and Pre-Appointment Firm Performance
detail.abstract: We examine whether performance expectations for a chief executive officer (CEO) are influenced by historical firm performance under a predecessor’s management. We find that the sensitivity of CEO turnover to contemporaneous performance increases in pre‑appointment firm performance. An underperforming CEO is more (less) likely to be dismissed when appointed at a firm with comparatively better (worse) pre‑appointment performance. Further, we find that the effect of pre-appointment performance increases when there are relatively few industry peers, and it declines over a CEO’s tenure. However, we do not find compelling evidence that our findings are attributable to the incumbent CEO’s ability, corporate governance quality, or CEO replacement costs. Overall, our findings suggest that CEO performance is assessed relative to that of their predecessors.

title: The ESG Disclosure Paradox Revisited: Integration of Environmental Justice Criteria

detail.title: The ESG Disclosure Paradox Revisited: Integration of Environmental Justice Criteria
detail.abstract:
In the Age of Information and climate disruption, businesses must navigate the perils of environmental degradation and deregulation and the unfolding of an informational and technological revolution. Under this context, companies can utilize innovative reporting frameworks to measure, assess, and disclose their environmental and social impacts, particularly on communities that have been historically and disproportionately affected by corporate decision-making.


This Article explores the paradox that lies at the intersection of two trending acronyms: Environmental Social and Governance (“ESG”) reporting, defined as a metric-driven approach to achieve corporate accountability and which can be imposed mandatorily by public law or voluntarily through Private Environmental Governance (“PEG”); and Environmental Justice (“EJ”), a social movement that denounces the unfair distribution of environmental impacts on vulnerable communities, and which has evolved into policies and sophisticated metrics and frameworks to assess inequalities in environmental harms caused by private and public decision-making.


Due to the current political attacks on environmental policies, mandatory ESG remains improbable. Thus, this Article analyzes how businesses are voluntarily disclosing environmental and social impacts. There are compelling reasons that justify the integration of EJ risks into sustainability reporting, including material climate-related risks, investor and consumer preferences, and achieving long-term corporate value. Corporate governance, related to corporate design, fiduciary duties, and the role of management, can adapt to integrate EJ considerations, redefining the rules and practices that shape shareholder-management relationships.


This Article argues that EJ risks and opportunities should be material for businesses to disclose. ESG reporting that integrates environmental justice objectives can also promote the long-term viability of a business. In the absence of public regulation, the integration of EJ into voluntary ESG frameworks offers an innovative interim solution for advancing environmental stewardship and responding to the urgent challenges of our time.

title: Algorithmic Colonialism: The Dawn of a New Era of Colonialism
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Algorithmic Colonialism: The Dawn of a New Era of Colonialism

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study did not involve human participants or patient data
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding

detail.abstract:
This paper traces the historical evolution of colonial practices, highlighting the transition from traditional military conquest to what is here conceptualized as algorithmic colonialism. Whereas the nineteenth and twentieth centuries were marked by territorial occupation, resource extraction, and political subjugation, the post–World War II order introduced subtler forms of domination through cultural industries such as Hollywood, global consumer brands, and Western universities. Globalization and transnational media reinforced this cultural hegemony, framing the world as a “global village” shaped by Western ideals.
In the digital era, these dynamics have intensified as algorithms emerged as infrastructures of governance. Far from neutral, they filter knowledge, shape public discourse, and predict individual behaviour. Platforms such as Google, Facebook, TikTok, and WeChat illustrate how digital ecosystems function as instruments of control—constructing filter bubbles, steering political debate, and commodifying personal data.
The paper argues that algorithmic colonialism represents the latest stage of global domination, one that colonizes perception and consciousness through code, platforms, and data flows. It concludes by emphasizing the urgent need for critical awareness, alternative infrastructures, and regulatory safeguards to protect epistemic autonomy and advance digital sovereignty in the twenty-first century.

title: Common Human Development Index: The Sense of Community Predicts Better Happiness
affiliations: University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics and University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Common Human Development Index: The Sense of Community Predicts Better Happiness
detail.abstract: The Human Development Index neglects the social dimension. This paper argues that a fundamental component for developing happiness is the sense of community and that, accordingly, Human Developmenttoward happiness-should include it along with life expectancy, education and income. By applying sufficient conditions logic maps we qualify the development stages from nit life satisfied to fully satisfied on a sample of 5000 Italians. Our findings reveal that high life satisfaction is prevented by bad health, low income and low sense of community. The latter is the only preventor also of medium-high levels of life satisfaction and adds significant explanatory power in multivariate life satisfaction estimates after controlling for HDI variables. Education has an indirect role by preventing having low sense of community, income, or health. Since sense of community is a preference and not an achievement or a state of affairs (such as income, health and education), our findings have relevant consequences in terms of rejection of the preference neutrality hypothesis.

title: The 'Suspended Step' of Damages Claims for Competition Law Infringements in Greece: An Institutional Odyssey
affiliations: University College London - Faculty of Laws and Independent

detail.title: The 'Suspended Step' of Damages Claims for Competition Law Infringements in Greece: An Institutional Odyssey

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Ioannis Lianos has been the President of the Hellenic Competition Commission between Sept. 2019 and Jan 2024 and the Chair of the special Law Commission for the revision of Greek Competition Law which ultimately led to Law 4886/2022. There is no other conflict of interest or any funding received for this paper to report.

detail.abstract: This study examines the 'suspended step' of competition damages claims in Greece, identifying multiple institutional constraints that hinder their development alongside underlying policy choices made during implementation of the EU Damages Directive and, more recently, the Directive on representative actions. These factors contribute to Greece's weak position in the inter-jurisdictional competition ‘game’ fostered by the EU legislator with the aim to ensure effective judicial protection for victims of anticompetitive conduct. Through empirical analysis combined with a law and political economy approach - a key innovation of this paper - the study examines both public and private enforcement of competition law, viewing them holistically. This methodology moves beyond traditional optimal enforcement theory to provide a uniquely comprehensive 'law in action' perspective on competition law enforcement institutional design. The findings offer valuable insights for all jurisdictions considering adoption of mixed public and private enforcement systems for competition law.

title: Is the 'Jungle' Really a Symbol of Chaos? A Response to Satirical Dismissals of Social Science
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Is the 'Jungle' Really a Symbol of Chaos? A Response to Satirical Dismissals of Social Science
detail.abstract: This paper challenges the satirical dismissal of social sciences as futile attempts to explain complexity, using the metaphor of the “jungle” as a central case. While satire often portrays the jungle as chaos and primal disorder, closer inspection reveals structured ecological laws, adaptive feedbacks, and even instances of compassion. Drawing on classical political theory (Hobbes), foundational sociology (Durkheim), and contemporary approaches such as complexity theory, analytical sociology, and the phronetic method, the paper demonstrates that what appears as disorder is frequently governed by hidden logics. By contrasting natural equilibrium with socially manufactured chaos—wars, injustice, and institutional failures—it argues that social sciences are indispensable for decoding complexity and guiding humane solutions. The essay concludes that the jungle is not chaos but law, while true disorder often stems from human misuse of power.

title: הלוך הלכו העצים: אמונאות, נבצרות ומלוכנות The Trees Went Forth: Fiduciary Obligations, Incapacity, and Royalism
affiliations: Reichman University

detail.title: הלוך הלכו העצים: אמונאות, נבצרות ומלוכנות The Trees Went Forth: Fiduciary Obligations, Incapacity, and Royalism
detail.abstract:
תקציר בעברית: תיקון מס' 12 לחוק־יסוד: הממשלה קובע כי נבצרות ראש הממשלה יכולה להיות פיזית בלבד, ובמשמע – כי אינה יכולה להיות נורמטיבית כגון מחמת ניגוד עניינים.  מאמר זה טוען כי תיקון זה ("תיקון הנבצרות") נגוע באי חוקתיות מחמת תוכנו המהותי, ועל כן הוא בטל מיסודו ולא רק נדחה בתחולתו.  זאת, בהיותו "שינוי חוקתי השולל את ליבת הזהות היהודית או הדמוקרטית של המדינה," כלשונה של הנשיאה חיות בעניין חסון נ' כנסת ישראל.  המאמר עומד על האופן שבו המשפט הציבורי בישראל נשען על מסגרת אמונאית לעיצוב חיוביהם של השלטון ואנשיו כלפי המדינה והציבור ועל מקומה של הצהרת האמונים בהקשר זה.  בהמשך המאמר מסביר את מקורותיו ואת נפקותו של מושג הנבצרות, אשר לא נדון לגופו בהליכים ביחס לתיקון הנבצרות.  לאור זאת נטען כי איון האפשרות לנבצרות מחמת ניגוד עניינים ביחס לראש הממשלה מכרסם בליבה הקשה של מעמדו המשפטי כאמונאי והופך אותו למעין-מלך, ועל כן הוא בטל.

English Abstract: Amendment No. 12 to Basic Law: The Government provides that the Prime Minister’s incapacity may be physical only, and by implication, excluding normative grounds such as a conflict of interest. This Article contends that the amendment (hereinafter: “the Incapacity Amendment”) is unconstitutional in its very substance and is consequently void ab initio, rather than having merely deferred voidness. This conclusion flows from its character as a “constitutional amendment that negates the core of the Jewish or democratic identity of the State,” in the words of President Hayut in Hasson v. The Knesset. The Article notes that Israeli public law is grounded in a fiduciary framework that defines the obligations of government and its officials vis-à-vis the State and the public, and underscores the centrality of the declaration of loyalty within that framework. It proceeds to examine the historical foundations and legal ramifications of the concept of disability, which were not substantively adjudicated in the litigation concerning the Incapacity Amendment. Against this background, the Article argues that the elimination of incapacity on the ground of conflict of interest, insofar as it pertains to the Prime Minister, erodes the very core of his fiduciary legal status and, in effect, transforms him into a quasi-monarch. Accordingly, the Amendment must be deemed void.

title: Representativeness Bias, Investment Decisions, and Financial Literacy of Selected Small and Medium Enterprises in Nairobi County
affiliations: Kisii University, Kisii University and Kisii University

detail.title: Representativeness Bias, Investment Decisions, and Financial Literacy of Selected Small and Medium Enterprises in Nairobi County
detail.abstract: Investment decisions are significantly affected by behavioral biases, potentially leading to suboptimal financial outcomes. Small and medium enterprises often make investment decisions based on heuristics like representativeness bias, leading to overestimation of asset performance and suboptimal financial outcomes. Given the critical role of financial literacy in mitigating such biases and promoting rational decision-making, there is a need for research to assess their effect on investment decisions. This study examined the mediating role of financial literacy in the relationship between representativeness bias and investment decisions of selected small and medium enterprises in Nairobi County. This study was based on Behavioral Portfolio Theory, Heuristics Theory, and Human Capital Theory. This study employed a positivist research philosophy utilizing a crosssectional and survey research design. A proportionate stratified random sampling was used to select a sample of 426 from 18,872 small and medium firms registered with the Micro and Small Enterprise Authority. The target respondents from each enterprise selected, managers or proprietors. Statistical Package for Social Sciences with Hayes Model 4 were used in data processing and analysis. Descriptive and inferential statistics were used to analyze data collected from the 376 respondents. Pearson correlation analysis revealed a weak statistically significant positive association between representativeness bias and financial literacy (r = 0.215, p = 0.000), as well as between representativeness bias and investment decisions (r = 0.149, p = 0.004). Financial literacy showed a strong positive connection with investing decisions (r = 0.981, p = 0.000). Mediation analysis indicated that representativeness bias adversely affected investment decisions (β =-0.0939, p < 0.05), whereas financial literacy attenuated this effect (indirect impact: 0.2928, p < 0.001). Bootstrap calculations corroborated these findings. The study concluded that financial literacy is essential in mitigating representativeness bias and advocated for structured decision-making frameworks and training programs for SMEs to improve their investment decisions.

reference: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series No. 237
title: Is Fedwire Still a Subsidy That Fully Recovers Its Cost?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago - Research Department

detail.title: Is Fedwire Still a Subsidy That Fully Recovers Its Cost?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series No. 237
publicationDetails.journalName: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the Federal Reserve's current financial losses-unprecedented in scale-and the questionable accounting practices it uses to downplay their impact. It argues that the Fed's self defined accounting standards, particularly the creation of a "deferred asset" to mask negative equity, obscure the fiscal consequences for the U.S. government and taxpayers. The analysis connects today's losses to longstanding institutional practices, notably the Fed's flawed cost recovery accounting for its Fedwire payment system. These issues first emerged in the late 1990s and early 2000s, when the author, then a Fed staffer, challenged the internal logic used to claim that Fedwire guaranteed payments and still avoided subsidies. The paper includes as an appendix the original 2002 draft, "Fedwire: A Subsidy That Fully Recovers Its Cost?", which helped reveal the moral hazard and accounting inconsistencies that contributed to the 2008 crisis and continue to shape central bank risk and governance today.

title: ABB_Industry_4.0_Transformation_2025
affiliations: NodesPay Tekh Pte Ltd

detail.title: ABB_Industry_4.0_Transformation_2025
detail.abstract: This report focuses on ABB Ltd's strategic adoption of Industry 4.0 (I4.0) technologies such as Blockchain, Big Data, Cloud Computing, and Cybersecurity towards its digital transformation journey and preparation for Industry 5.0 (I5.0). By using case study and analysis, this paper explores ABB's approach toward the integration of I4.0 technologies, overcoming implementation challenges, and ensuring resilience towards innovation. The report further provides insights into strategy approaches that ABB uses, like technology investment and partnership. Finally, the report ends with recommendations towards ABB's further adoption of I4.0 technologies and I5.0 practices, which focus on human-centric and ethical principles to gain competitive advantages in the market.

title: Sacrifice And Social Cohesion in the Fourth Verse of the Anthem
affiliations: EDUKIVOTOS

detail.title: Sacrifice And Social Cohesion in the Fourth Verse of the Anthem
detail.abstract: The fourth verse of the Colombian National Anthem, which evokes the resilience of the people of Cartagena in the face of siege and adversity, constitutes a symbolic symbol of social cohesion and collective sacrifice. This study, based on Émile Durkheim's theory of social solidarity and cultural transmission approaches, analyzes how the lyrics of the anthem transcend generations to shape senses of belonging, national identity, and institutional legitimacy. The paper argues that the exaltation of sacrifice, selflessness, and contempt for death become elements of collective memory that influence the relationship between citizens and public administration, strengthening legitimacy in contemporary governance.

title: Trade Balance and Exchange Rate Dynamics: J-Curve Phenomenon Revisit
affiliations: Momoyama Gakuin University, Kansai University and Chukyo University

detail.title: Trade Balance and Exchange Rate Dynamics: J-Curve Phenomenon Revisit
detail.abstract: This study revisits the J-curve phenomenon in a small open economy new Keynesian model. The main findings are summarized as follows. First, a higher degree of habit persistence is essential to generate an empirically plausible J-curve response following an unanticipated terms of trade shock. Second, given a high degree of habit formation, the J-curve arises when exchange rate pass-through is predominantly incomplete. Third, an anticipated terms of trade shock can also generate a J-curve pattern; however, this effect disappears under a high degree of habit persistence. Finally, the specification of the monetary policy rule is not essential in generating the J-curve effect.

title: National Symbols and Social Cohesion in Colombia (1836)
affiliations: EDUKIVOTOS

detail.title: National Symbols and Social Cohesion in Colombia (1836)
detail.abstract: This paper presents a sociological, anthropological, and semiotic analysis of the 1836 National Song , written by Pombo and set to music by José Caicedo Rojas, in its role in the construction of Colombian identity. Drawing on the postulates of Émile Durkheim and theories of cultural transmission, the paper examines the symbolic value of the lyrics as a vehicle for social cohesion and political legitimacy in the practices of governing and being governed. The study interprets how this precursor anthem, transmitted through generations, impacts the solidity of national identity, projecting a symbol of unity in the face of globalization and contemporary territorial challenges.

title: Minimize Regret
affiliations: AbleMarkets.com

detail.title: Minimize Regret
detail.abstract: Using the representation of regret as a covariance between inputs and outputs in any machine learning system (Aldridge (2025)), this article develops conditions to minimize regret.

title: Organizational Blindness and Paralysis in the Face of Disruption: A Sensemaking Perspective
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Leicester and University of Turku - Copenhagen Business School

detail.title: Organizational Blindness and Paralysis in the Face of Disruption: A Sensemaking Perspective
detail.abstract: This paper builds on research that examines the sensemaking dynamics behind a phenomenon where some incumbents fail to respond to visible disruption despite having access to abundant resources and early warning signals. Drawing on data collected during a multi-year project, the study uses Weick’s sensemaking theory as a conceptual framework, and adopts a methodology inspired by Grounded Theory to investigate two interpretive failures: organizational blindness (failing to perceive disruption threats) and organizational paralysis (failing to act on perceived disruption threats). The findings reveal and connect a number of recurring organizational dynamics that inhibit appropriate response. A four-phase model of interpretive failure is developed to explain how visibility of disruption does not guarantee organizational action. This study contributes to innovation literature by extending sensemaking theory to account for internal misalignments in structure, identity, and corporate dynamics.

title: On the Optimal Design of Consumption Taxes
affiliations: European University Institute

detail.title: On the Optimal Design of Consumption Taxes
detail.abstract: This paper studies the optimal design of differentiated consumption taxes in the presence of progressive labor income taxes and capital income taxation. A quantitative heterogeneousagent model with non-homothetic preferences and uninsurable idiosyncratic risk is estimated using US consumption and price data to match expenditure patterns across the income distribution. Solving the Ramsey problem in which the government jointly chooses labor income and commodity taxes, the optimal policy prescribes a subsidy on necessities of-52% and a positive tax of 7% on luxuries, accompanied by a reduction in labor tax progressivity. Three mechanisms account for these results: subsidized necessities provide consumption insurance, taxation of luxuries acts as an implicit tax on existing wealth, and differentiated rates strengthen labor supply incentives among highly productive households.

title: Childcare Costs, Investments, and Savings of Young Families
affiliations: George Mason University

detail.title: Childcare Costs, Investments, and Savings of Young Families

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I do not have any personal or financial relationships that could have influenced the results of this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: My study did not require this type of information.
declarations.funderStatement: I received no external funding for this project.

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of childcare costs on young families' homeownership and retirement savings decisions. Using a regression discontinuity design based on public school eligibility rules, I identify the impact of additional childcare expenses on families whose children miss the kindergarten cutoff date. I find evidence that families who miss the cutoff are 3.5% less likely to become homeowners, purchase homes 1.8% lower in value, and are 17.5% less likely to contribute to retirement savings compared to those who enroll their children in public school a year earlier. These findings suggest that high childcare costs, which typically consume between 11% to 36% of a family's income, may delay wealthaccumulating investments during early career years. By emphasizing the role of childcare expenses in wealth accumulation, this research links childcare policy with potential long-term impacts on household financial stability.

title: The Fed Put and Bank Risk-Taking: Evidence from the Loan Book
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, University of Münster, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business and

detail.title: The Fed Put and Bank Risk-Taking: Evidence from the Loan Book
detail.abstract: This paper shows that monetary policy influences bank credit policy through the risk taking channel. Using option prices on FOMC announcement days, we measure the impact of monetary policy on bank equity tail risks and link them to loan-level regulatory data. Banks that experience a decline in tail risk lend more to riskier firms and ease loan terms in the three weeks after the FOMC. These effects are concentrated among banks with short-term compensation structures and in competitive credit markets. Our results isolate the impact of bank risk-taking in loan supply from confounding forces such as endogenous credit demand and highlight how institutional frictions mediate the risk-taking channel of monetary policy.

title: Management Disclosure and Media Coverage
affiliations: EDHEC Business School and University of Groningen - Faculty of Economics and Business

detail.title: Management Disclosure and Media Coverage
detail.abstract: We examine how management disclosure affects media coverage by analyzing firms' responses in earnings call Q&A sessions. Using a machine-learning-based "non-answer" score, we find that evasive managerial responses reduce subsequent media attention, particularly from professional outlets generating original content. This supports a supply-driven view of media coverage: poor disclosure limits journalistic content creation. Reduced coverage, in turn, is associated with lower investor engagement and weaker stock performance. Our findings highlight the critical role of a firm's information environment in shaping the level and nature of subsequent media coverage, with implications for broader financial market outcomes.

title: Contracting against Non-contractible Outsider
affiliations: Yale University, Department of Economics

detail.title: Contracting against Non-contractible Outsider
detail.abstract: This paper studies contracting in the presence of externalities with a non-contractible outsider. Multiple equilibria arise from strategic symmetry between the insider agent and the outsider. To address strategic uncertainty, the principal guarantees their actions in a unique equilibrium. A novel duality approach reformulates her problem as a series of problems in which she selects agent expectations. The key constraint is that the principal cannot convince the agent to expect non-guaranteed response from the outsider. Due to strategic rents, the principal optimally induces attenuated agent incentives. With completely symmetric strategic dependence, her coordination and commitment power become perfect substitutes; in addition, public contracting can strictly decrease her surplus compared to private contracting, in sharp contrast with the case where she ignores robustness. Applications include regulating international competition, platform design, and labor union contracting.

title: Tipping Points: Fear, Nonlinear Comovement, and the Global Pricing Kernel
affiliations: HEC Montreal - Department of Finance

detail.title: Tipping Points: Fear, Nonlinear Comovement, and the Global Pricing Kernel
detail.abstract: We find that the asset pricing literatures generally accepted positive relation between fear measures and international correlations masks strong nonlinearities. Using daily data for 37 countries, we find this relationship is, on average, convex (U-shaped), with correlations decreasing before an economically important "tipping point." Cross-sectionally, this convexity is more pronounced in countries with higher inflation and deeper financial integration, linking it to intermediary and macroeconomic channels. Furthermore, time-varying Markov-switching models confirm that fear nonlinearly increases the probability of entering a high-correlation regime. These patterns provide evidence on state-dependent exposures to the global pricing kernel, consistent with a unified structural model.

title: Pricing Fiscal Gains and Externalities: The Effects of Shale Booms on Municipal Finance
affiliations: Rice University - Jesse H. Jones Graduate School of Business, Rice University - Jesse H. Jones Graduate School of Business and

detail.title: Pricing Fiscal Gains and Externalities: The Effects of Shale Booms on Municipal Finance
detail.abstract: Using geographic and temporal variation in shale discoveries and drilling incentives, we show that municipalities exposed to shale booms experience lower municipal borrowing costs and improved creditworthiness. Four mechanisms explain these effects: tax revenues, municipal expenditure, environmental costs, and public safety. Revenue surpluses enable local governments to reduce reliance on bond markets to finance capital. The fiscal benefits are more pronounced in economically disadvantaged municipalities, where the marginal value of resource windfalls is greater. Our findings suggest that investors perceive the fiscal gains from fracking as outweighing its negative externalities, and these opposing forces are capitalized into municipal bond markets.

title: A Realistic, Heterogeneous (Principal-) Agent Asset Pricing Model: With Asset Allocation and Risk-Adjusted Performance
affiliations: Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business

detail.title: A Realistic, Heterogeneous (Principal-) Agent Asset Pricing Model: With Asset Allocation and Risk-Adjusted Performance
detail.abstract:
The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), based on investors/principals, maximizing their expected utility of wealth, assumed a single representative investor and a deterministic goal/liability. Subsequent heterogenous agent asset pricing models (HAPMs) were based on trivial variations to utility functions/preferences, and market frictions, but, in reality, there are no well-specified "utility functions", or "risk-aversion" parameters (and probably HAPMs incorrectly use "agent" instead of "participant" or "principal"). Prof. Cochrane has suggested that, "Switching to a payoff perspective may change lots of procedures in finance", and we use his approach to propose a realistic HAPM that corrects for these challenges.

Three variations of realistic heterogeneity in markets are explored instead in this model: (i) heterogeneity of cash flows of different investment goals (retirement; kid’s education, buying a house, etc.); (ii) heterogeneity of cash flows within a goal, based on different ages of investors that impact cash flow start/end dates and duration; and (iii) heterogeneity of clearly articulated relative risk targets for delegation. The proposed model incorporates four realities of investing; (i) that investors/principals have many stochastic goals (i.e., cash flows or payoffs they desire), and that is the primary example of real-life heterogeneity; (ii) they seek to delegate to skillful agents (in the true academic sense of the word); (iii) explicitly specify risk preferences (adding in an additional layer of heterogeneity); and (iv) maximize risk-adjusted relative returns. In this HAPM, assets are priced with just two goal-replicating assets (issued by Brazil in 2023), and the absolute risk-free asset. The pair-wise equilibrium model uses observable assets and risk preferences parameters, eliminates "free parameters", and lends itself to a general equilibrium model of assets and wages too. Critical to investment practice, it provides asset pricing, asset allocations and risk-adjusted performance measures that are consistent. It offers a new pathway to a realistic HAPM.

title: The Economic Costs of Mass Shootings: Evidence from U.S. Housing Markets
affiliations: Stevens Institute of Technology and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: The Economic Costs of Mass Shootings: Evidence from U.S. Housing Markets
detail.abstract: We study the impact of mass shootings on local housing markets using ZIP-level monthly data from 2017-2023 and a matched-control design. Following an incident, markets cool as buyer interest diminishes and sellers respond with slower listings, longer time on market, and greater price concessions. Listing prices decline, showing that weaker demand outweighs any temporary supply pullback. These effects extend the household finance literature by demonstrating that highly salient, extreme forms of gun violence trigger immediate demand-supply adjustments that erode housing-market liquidity and home values. Mass shootings thus impose significant economic costs, reducing household wealth and weakening local resilience beyond their human toll.

title: Do Monetary Policy Rules and Inflation Influence Tariff Dynamics in Sahel and Sahara Countries? A Tobit Model Approach
affiliations: Sudan University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Do Monetary Policy Rules and Inflation Influence Tariff Dynamics in Sahel and Sahara Countries? A Tobit Model Approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: approval
declarations.ethicsApproval: approval
declarations.funderStatement: approval

detail.abstract: This paper looks at the relationship between monetary policy rules, inflation, and tariff dynamics in Sahel and Sahara countries from 1980-2024. Using a Tobit panel regression methodology to account for the censored character of tariff data, the analysis analyzes how macroeconomic stabilization programs affect trade policy outcomes. The findings show that tariffs respond considerably to monetary and inflationary situations. Tariffs increase in response to exchange rate depreciation and inflation (CPI), emphasizing both defensive and revenue-generating responsibilities. Monetary expansion (M2), government consumption, and interest rates are all positively associated with higher tariffs, indicating fiscal reliance on trade taxes and the complementary nature of monetary tightening and protectionist measures. Improving the current account reduces reliance on tariffs, which is consistent with their counter-cyclical usage in balance-of-payments management. The findings highlight tariffs' dual significance as trade policy instruments and macroeconomic stabilizers in Africa's fragile and shock-prone economies. Policy recommendations focus on improving currency rate management, minimizing inflationary pressures, diversifying fiscal revenue sources, and aligning tariff reforms with regional integration initiatives under the AFCFTA.

title: Total Returns of US Treasury Index Funds Derived from Bond Prices Between 1941 and 1982
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Total Returns of US Treasury Index Funds Derived from Bond Prices Between 1941 and 1982
detail.abstract: The prices and amounts in issue of US notes and bonds recorded in the Treasury Bulletin between the end of 1941 and 1982 have been used to calculate the returns, weighted yields, and weighted durations of various indices (e.g., maturities of 1 to 3 years, 1 to 5 years, etc.). Changes in the tax status of treasuries across these four decades meant that three different versions of each index, all bonds, fully taxable only, and tax exempt only were calculated. The annualised returns over the four decades differed by no more than 25 bp from those in existing datasets, while the median magnitude of differences in annual returns lay between 0.2 and 1.2 percentage points depending on the dataset being compared. However, in some years the differences in the annual returns were up to 5 pp, the reasons for which have been explored in detail. The annual returns were also compared with those derived from yield curves with median differences of less than 1 pp, although much larger differences of up to 6.5 pp occurred when the synthetic bond market derived from the yield curves was at variance with the historical bond market.

title: Computational Learning Mechanisms of Information Propagating in Social Networks
affiliations: , Dartmouth College - Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, EMLYON Business School and Claude Bernard Lyon 1 University

detail.title: Computational Learning Mechanisms of Information Propagating in Social Networks
detail.abstract: What mechanisms underlie how individuals integrate disparate and redundant information that spreads in social networks? The DeGroot (DG) model suggests that we adjust our beliefs according to the weighted average opinions of our social connections. In contrast, reinforcement learning (RL) models assume that learning occurs sequentially, depending on error-driven belief updating. Here, we compare these models directly using two datasets of information propagating in social networks, and determine which learning rule best accounts for the integration of information spreading in social networks. We found that variants of the DG model provide a better overall fit across participants, and are more effective in building consensus, and generating accurate estimates of the true state of the world. Furthermore, simulated models show how social network topology affects choice accuracy and consensus, depending on the learning rule. Together, our findings characterize the computational mechanisms used by individuals to propagate information in social networks.

title: Human Capital Accumulation, Chapter 6, The Making of Korea’s Liberty and Prosperity
affiliations: Yeungnam University

detail.title: Human Capital Accumulation, Chapter 6, The Making of Korea’s Liberty and Prosperity
detail.abstract: This chapter clarifies the interaction between human capital accumulation and economic growth and between public provision of education and private demand for learning, focusing on the rise of Korean literacy and primary schooling up to 1960. The first section begins by outlining the path of Korean human capital accumulation to highlight that it sped up significantly with the 1945 decolonization. The second and third sections analyze the literacy improvement and the advance of primary schooling in the half century leading up to 1945. Section 4 discusses how the 1945 de-colonization caused literacy and primary education to surge in South Korea. The last section concludes by highlighting that the rapid accumulation of Korean human capital occurred against the backdrop of the transition from limited to open-access order.

title: Incentives in Competition: The Role of Money, Recognition, and Perception in Performance
affiliations: State Bank of Pakistan and Akhuwat University

detail.title: Incentives in Competition: The Role of Money, Recognition, and Perception in Performance
detail.abstract: This study examines the comparative effectiveness of monetary and non-monetary incentives in competitive tournament-based remuneration structures. While prior research has demonstrated the superior efficiency of non-monetary incentives in cooperative or gift-exchange settings, our experimental results show that their relative advantage diminishes under competitive tournament conditions. Average output levels did not differ significantly between monetary and non-monetary treatments, suggesting that the social-relational benefits of non-monetary rewards are less effective when embedded in market-oriented competition. However, the analysis of shirking behavior reveals a contrasting dynamic: monetary tournaments generated significantly higher shirking, whereas non-monetary tournaments reduced it. Moreover, labor supply decisions in monetary treatments were strongly shaped by participants' perceptions of relative competitiveness, leading to polarized performance outcomes. Perception was found to be primarily skill-based, but psychological responses also played a crucial role. Non-monetary incentives, while equal in productivity, offered advantages in reducing shirking, lowering expected disappointment, and enhancing job satisfaction. These findings highlight that incentive effectiveness depends not only on the type of reward but also on the structure in which it is implemented.

title: The fire that does not go out: the neglected costs of gas flaring in Nigeria
affiliations: World Bank Group and The University of Waikato

detail.title: The fire that does not go out: the neglected costs of gas flaring in Nigeria
detail.abstract: Gas flaring, the burning of gas coming out of oil wells is a common practice in oil-producing developing countries. This practice is harmful to human health, especially because of pollutants. This research focuses on Nigeria, where over 10 percent of all gas produced is flared and about two million people are estimated to live within four kilometres of a flare site. This paper uses infant health data from Demographic Health Surveys, and satellite-detected data on gas flaring to examine the effects of flaring on disease incidence and infant mortality in oil-producing regions. The findings show a strong positive association between flaring and the incidence of respiratory diseases and fever among children under five years old. The study contributes to the literature measuring the wider cost to society of oil and gas production and adds to the body of work using satellite data to understand well-being in places where conventional data sources are unavailable.

title: Juxtaposing the Global Citizenship Competencies of Senior High School and College Students: Input for a Contextualized Learning Plan
affiliations: Department of Education, Republic of the Philippines and Bataan Peninsula State University, Bataan, Philippines

detail.title: Juxtaposing the Global Citizenship Competencies of Senior High School and College Students: Input for a Contextualized Learning Plan
detail.abstract: Education and globalization, as tools empowering learners to think and act globally, are driving forces for producing the competent and humanized citizens that the world needs today. The present study explores the global citizenship competencies of senior high school (SHS) and college students as the baseline for a contextualized learning plan premised on that. The study employs the descriptive survey design of quantitative research, wherein the needed data are gathered through a questionnaire to select students with leadership positions in various student organizations in their respective institutions. The data gathered are analyzed using descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviation) and inferential statistics (Independent Samples t-test). The findings reveal that both SHS and college students show strong agreement in possessing global citizenship competencies across knowledge, skills, values, and attitudes, with college students exhibiting slightly higher levels. College students demonstrate significantly more vital global citizenship competencies in knowledge, values, attitudes, and overall domains than SHS students, while no significant difference is observed in the skills domain. A contextualized learning plan is developed to address the learning needs of SHS and college students, aiming to sustain and enhance their global citizenship competencies in knowledge, values, and attitudes through various tailored activities.

title: Movement Lawyers: Henry L. Marsh's Long Struggle For Educational Justice

detail.title: Movement Lawyers: Henry L. Marsh's Long Struggle For Educational Justice
detail.abstract:
Even with Virginia’s critical importance to the national Civil Rights Movement, there remains little legal scholarship that centers the humanist social histories of Virginia’s civil rights lawyers. Existing work on civil rights, education, and Massive Resistance has emphasized state-level politics, judicial rulings, and a handful of prominent figures. Historians have analyzed Virginia’s legal approach to desegregation and key leaders, but they have largely overlooked the everyday experiences and strategies of Black Virginia lawyers who fought Massive Resistance on the ground.

This Article seeks to fill that gap by documenting the lived experiences and legal practices of these lawyers, focusing in particular on Henry L. Marsh. Scholarship on the NAACP’s school desegregation litigation is well established, but less attention has been paid to what that work looked like in day-to-day practice, the methods lawyers employed, and the continuing significance of those methods today. Marsh’s professional and personal life provides a rich site for this inquiry. By offering a nuanced analysis of his career and commitments, this Article expands our understanding of Virginia’s civil rights history and highlights the enduring relevance of movement lawyering to contemporary struggles for educational justice.

title: Challenges in Scope Management: Trends, Gaps, and Implications for Project Success
affiliations: University of Johannesburg, Johannesburg, South Africa and University of Johannesburg, Johannesburg, South Africa

detail.title: Challenges in Scope Management: Trends, Gaps, and Implications for Project Success
detail.abstract: Scope management is widely recognized as a critical determinant of project success, yet its practices, applications, and outcomes vary significantly across industries and project types. Existing literature provides fragmented insights, with limited emphasis on methodological consistency and emerging technological solutions. This review synthesizes evidence from 2015 to 2025 to (i) identify prevalent approaches to scope management, (ii) assess their impact on project success, (iii) examine variations across industries and regulatory frameworks, and (iv) highlight methodological gaps and future research opportunities. A systematic search of Google Scholar, Web of Science, and Scopus retrieved 1,180 records. After duplicate removal and screening, 46 studies were included. Study characteristics, methodological quality, regulatory frameworks, and technological applications were analyzed. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. The final pool comprised literature reviews (43.48%), journal papers (17.39%), surveys (17.39%), systematic reviews (10.87%), interviews (6.53%), case studies (2.17%), and academic journals (2.17%). Most studies (82.61%) achieved moderate-to-high quality ratings. Project management software dominated (58.70%), strongly associated with cost reduction, quality assurance, and timeline adherence. Digital collaboration tools (28.26%) enhanced stakeholder involvement and interdepartmental coordination, while AI-driven risk assessment (10.87%) showed promise in predictive and preventive project management. Sectoral imbalances were evident, with infrastructure overrepresented and healthcare/IT underrepresented. Regulatory adoption was uneven, with PMBOK frequently applied, while ISO 21500 remained underutilized. Scope management practices contribute significantly to project success, but gaps persist in methodological rigor, sectoral diversity, and the exploration of emerging technologies. Future studies should expand beyond infrastructure, adopt standardized frameworks, and test digital and AI-enhanced tools. Practitioners are encouraged to integrate traditional documentation approaches with collaborative and predictive technologies to improve project outcomes.

title: Transforming UAE's Supply Chain Management through Artificial Intelligence: Case Studies and Insights
affiliations: Symbiosis International University - Symbiosis Centre for Information Technology (SCIT) and Independent author

detail.title: Transforming UAE's Supply Chain Management through Artificial Intelligence: Case Studies and Insights
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly integral to the United Arab Emirates' (UAE) vision of a diversified, high-tech economy. This research examines how AI is transforming supply chain management (SCM) in the UAE, driven by ambitious national strategies and multi-billion-dollar investments. We review the UAE's AI Strategy 2031 and its emphasis on logistics, then analyze several case studies-both government-led and private-to illustrate core AI applications in supply chains. Key use-cases include predictive demand forecasting, route optimization, predictive maintenance, and automation in logistics and retail. For example, AI-driven demand forecasting helps firms avoid under-or over-stocking, while autonomous logistics platforms like Dubai's Blink optimize routing and trade flows. Abu Dhabi's Advanced Trade and Logistics Platform (ATLP) integrates AI for real-time tracking and predictive analytics, cutting documentation by 90% and halving processing times. We find that AI implementations have yielded significant efficiency gains-from inventory cost reductions to faster deliveries-and are projected to add around AED 335 billion (~$91 billion) to the UAE economy by 2031. However, challenges persist in technology procurement, talent acquisition, data governance, and aligning with evolving geopolitical constraints. Using a qualitative case study methodology (with a Gioia coding approach for thematic analysis), we identify critical success factors such as clear needs assessment in public AI procurement and robust public-private partnerships. This paper offers insights and recommendations for UAE policymakers and industry leaders: pursue pilot-first implementations, strengthen the local AI talent pipeline (e.g. via MBZUAI), and ensure ethical and sustainable AI adoption. In conclusion, while AI is demonstrably transforming the UAE's supply chain landscape through enhanced efficiency and innovation, continued strategic oversight is required to address challenges and fully realize AI's potential in driving economic growth and competitiveness.

title: The Promise and Perils of Enterprise Data as Trade Secrets
affiliations: School of Law, City University of Hong Kong

detail.title: The Promise and Perils of Enterprise Data as Trade Secrets
detail.abstract:
Various types of information, whether physically embodied or existing purely in digital form, can subsist as data, ready for collection and use by relevant actors. A broad distinction, however, may be drawn between personal data, derived from individuals, and enterprise data, which typically comprises large-scale collections generated or acquired by firms during business operations. Enterprise data may include proprietary business information as well as personal and non-personal data collected from external sources such as customers or the public. A growing body of literature explores legal frameworks for protecting enterprise data, though the approaches vary. Jurisdictions worldwide have not reached a consensus on whether or how enterprise data may receive legal protection, despite vigorous debates. An emerging viewpoint across jurisdictions is protecting enterprise data as trade secrets. However, acceptance of the concept of enterprise data as trade secrets remains uncertain.

This article engages with this debate and contributes to the current literature on enterprise data as trade secrets from three perspectives. First, it reiterates the potential promise of trade secrets law by offering a doctrinal analysis showing how trade secrets law is resilient to protect diverse forms of enterprise data in the data economy, including three key categories in the form of purely confidential enterprise data, private data compilations, and “semi-public” enterprise data compilations. Second, this article, filling the literature gap, explores current cases, laws, and regulations in representative jurisdictions, the US, China, and the EU, documenting the extent to which the concept of enterprise data as trade secrets has been recognized. This positive analysis  highlights the status quo: the role of trade secrets law in protecting the first two categories of enterprise data has gained growing and continuous recognition, but its application to “semi‑public” enterprise data compilations remains limited. Third, based on the positive exploration, the article unpacks the challenges and risks associated with applying trade secrets law to “semi-public” enterprise data compilations, offering explanations for its limited acceptance compared to the other two types. It argues that protecting most “semi-public” data compilations as trade secrets does not serve the core theoretical aims of trade secrets law. This is because extending protection to these compilations fails to yield the business efficiency necessary to justify the associated costs. Thus, normatively, the article argues that trade secrets law should only protect the type of “semi-public” data compilation whose front-end access is meaningfully restricted to a limited number of users. At the same time, trade secrets law cannot be used to sanction data scraping activities that do not involve intrusion into a data holder’s system or direct circumvention of genuine access restrictions.

title: The Relationship between IoT-Based Information Integration, Decision-Making Uncertainty, and Supply Chain Performance
affiliations: Cranfield University - School of Management, Cranfield University - School of Management and Cranfield University - School of Management

detail.title: The Relationship between IoT-Based Information Integration, Decision-Making Uncertainty, and Supply Chain Performance
detail.abstract: This paper explores the interplay between the Internet of Things (IoT)-based information integration and decision-making uncertainty and their combined impact on supply chain performance. Survey data on 275 supply chain managers is analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling to illustrate these relationships. IoT-based information integration and decisionmaking uncertainty is found to be a complex interaction between information accuracy, quality and efficiency; environmental complexity and richness; and demand distortion. The interactions between these factors partially mediate supply chain performance on cost management and production operations. This study provides empirical evidence for the information processing theorybased conceptualisation of the interaction between IoT-based information integration and decision-making uncertainty, and their interactions have a partial mediating role in improving supply chain performance. The research findings help supply chain managers develop a performance-oriented supply chain evaluation system to forecast the outcomes of implementing IoT-based information integration.

title: Budget Allocation for Utility Loss Minimization in Social Welfare Programs
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management

detail.title: Budget Allocation for Utility Loss Minimization in Social Welfare Programs
detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Social welfare programs (e.g., healthcare insurance, social security assistance) play an indispensable role in modern societies. In these programs, a social planner needs to allocate limited budget to minimize agents' utility loss associated with adverse events. We formulate this as an optimization problem and solve the optimal allocation policy.

Methodology/results: We find that the optimal allocation policy has a cap structure, in which all excess loss above a universal threshold is covered. We also solve the optimal ratio allocation policy by developing a priority index for each loss event. We explore two practically relevant issues in the budget allocation: horizontal heterogeneity across groups and intertemporal trade-off across periods. For the first issue, we investigate the effects of pooling when there are multiple groups. We find that with the optimal cap policy or under homogeneous loss distributions, it is optimal to integrate all groups with a common policy. For the second issue, we develop a dynamic model in which the social planner balances between spending for current period and saving for the future.  We reveal a piecewise-concave pattern of the optimal spending amount: the marginal spending rate for current period decreases in the fund level when the coverage scope is fixed, but experiences upward jumps when the coverage scope is expanded. The managerial insights are illustrated by numerical experiments and a case study based on actual data.

Managerial implications: We develop a unified framework for the budget allocation decision in social welfare programs, which are essential to achieve the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Our analytical results provide actionable insights for the integration and sustainability of welfare programs, which are major reform goals of many developing countries.

title: Rushed Justice: The Value of Fast-Track Dispute Systems on Second-Hand Platforms
affiliations: Rice University and Nanyang Business School, Nanyang Technological University

detail.title: Rushed Justice: The Value of Fast-Track Dispute Systems on Second-Hand Platforms
detail.abstract: Problem Definition: Buyers on secondhand platforms often face uncertainties related to product quality, which frequently leads to disputes with sellers. Therefore, online dispute resolution systems (ODR) play a critical role not only in facilitating transactions, but also in influencing how sellers manage product quality. This paper investigates how different ODR system designs affect the users and the overall platform performance. Methodology/Results: We utilize a game-theoretic model to analyze two prevalent ODR system designs: Swift ODR, which streamlines dispute resolution with minimal seller involvement, and Comprehensive ODR, which requires active participation from both the seller and the buyer in resolving dispute. Our results demonstrate that Swift ODR can incentivize sellers to maintain higher product quality, which improves consumer welfare, even when its accuracy in resolving disputes is lower than that of Comprehensive ODR. Moreover, we find that the platform benefits more from Swift ODR if there is a sufficiently high proportion of honest sellers. Interestingly, we also find that Swift ODR can be preferable in a platform with fewer honest sellers under certain combinations of commission rates and judging accuracy. Managerial Implications: Our findings suggest that a simpler and less accurate dispute system can have the potential to deliver higher product quality, greater platform profit, and improved consumer welfare. Platforms should strategically design their ODR systems by closely evaluating the market compositions, the accuracy of dispute resolutions, and commission structures.

title: Loglinear and Linear Approximate Solutions for Finite-Time Consumption-Investment Problem
affiliations: Shiga University and Shiga University

detail.title: Loglinear and Linear Approximate Solutions for Finite-Time Consumption-Investment Problem
detail.abstract: Assuming a quadratic security market model and homotopic robust utility in the finite-time consumption-investment problem, a secondorder nonhomogeneous nonlinear partial differential equation is derived. This study introduces two types of time-dependent loglinear approximation methods related to the nonhomogeneous term and four types of time-dependent linear approximation methods for the nonlinear term. The study derives loglinear approximate solutions and showcases the results of linear approximate solutions. The study then compares the approximation accuracies of the approximate optimal portfolios based on these approximate solutions. The numerical analysis indicates that the accuracies of both loglinear approximate optimal portfolios are very low, whereas those of all linear approximate optimal portfolios are very high.
