title: Art as Collateral: Toward an International Register for Artwork
affiliations: Fordham University School of Law and International University of Monaco (IUM)

detail.title: Art as Collateral: Toward an International Register for Artwork

keywords: UNI-DROIT Convention on Stolen or Illegally Exported Cultural Objects value

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in Berkeley Business Law Journal, vol. 26, iss. 2
Fordham Law Legal Studies Research Paper;
publicationDetails.journalName: Fordham Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In the last decades, a trend of art being used as a security in finance has emerged. The use of art as collateral for loans has become widespread, especially in the United States. However, this market practice is not without challenges. The valuation of art is often unstable and hard to predict, thus creating uncertainty for lenders. Buyers and lenders frequently must contend with unclear chains of title, thus exposing them to the risk of loss of value in artwork and even loss of legal title. This article explores the advantages and disadvantages of the rising use of art as collateral and proposes reforms to help the market reach higher levels of transparency, efficiency, and stability. Overall, the benefits of arts as collateral are manifold, including capitalization of the art market, expanding the art clientele as well as pushing technical boundaries in the securitization of art. At the same time, in light of a lack of legal certainty across borders, we propose the introduction of an obligatory international register for artwork that would record transactions in valuable art when security interests are at stake. A register should specify the artwork in detail and record documents conferring title, establishing security interests, and the basis for valuation. Such a register would have three significant advantages for the art market. First, it would improve legal certainty for art buyers and lenders accepting art as collateral. Second, it would standardize pricing of art by facilitating comparisons across time and between different works of art, but also around the globe. Thus, valuation would become simpler and subject to less uncertainty. Third, it would make it easier for governments to locate valuable national heritage in art for regulatory purposes and hinder money laundering and tax evasion.

title: From Cooperation to Anomie and Transaction in the Transatlantic Relationship? A View from Europe on the Trump Administration 2.0
affiliations: University of Hamburg, Law School

detail.title: From Cooperation to Anomie and Transaction in the Transatlantic Relationship? A View from Europe on the Trump Administration 2.0

declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: Alexander von Humboldt Foundation

detail.abstract: This paper discusses a European view on the Trump Administration 2.0 actions in the international realm. The focus is on the structural issues that affect Europe deeply. Although the whole world is concerned by these actions, for Europe, having been a close U.S. partner in the last eighty years, this is especially disappointing and disrupting. Not only is there disappointed trust but also a realization that formerly common shared values are no more. I focus on three themes: (1) U.S. actions paralyzing multilateralism, demonstrating a zero-sum thinking and free-riding on the provision of global public goods and commons; (2) U.S. ignoring central pillars of international law; and (3) U.S. destabilization of Europe itself through political meddling.

title: Evaluating the Implementation of the 20-Valent Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine for Paediatric Immunization in Australia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Evaluating the Implementation of the 20-Valent Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine for Paediatric Immunization in Australia
detail.abstract: Objective: In Australia, the paediatric national immunization programme (NIP) currently includes 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) under 2+1 schedule. The 15-valent (PCV15) and 20-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCV20) are available in Australia but not yet NIP funded. This cost-effectiveness analysis compared the public health and economic impact of implementing PCV20 into the Australian paediatric NIP versus PCV13 and PCV15.Methods: We conducted the cost-effectiveness analysis from the payer perspective using a population-based multi-cohort model with a 10-year horizon and a 5% annual discount rate for costs and benefits. The model considered direct vaccine effects in the vaccinated cohort aged <2 years and indirect effects in unvaccinated individuals of all ages. Input data for epidemiology, costs, and utilities were obtained from Australia-specific sources. Vaccine effectiveness inputs were derived from PCV13 real-world effectiveness data, 7-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV7) efficacy data, and PCV13 impact data. Model estimated pneumococcal disease cases (invasive pneumococcal disease, pneumonia, and otitis media), deaths, costs, and quality-adjusted life years (QALY) for each vaccination strategy, which were used to calculate incremental cost-effectiveness ratios. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to test uncertainty in input parameters and examine model robustness.Results: Model estimated that PCV20 implementation would prevent more disease cases and deaths than PCV13 (642,804 and 8,308, respectively) and PCV15 (290,943 and 3,730, respectively) over 10 years. PCV20 was associated with QALY gains of 117,417 and 55,279, and total cost-savings of AUD 668,174,379 and AUD 312,296,604 versus PCV13 and PCV15, respectively. Therefore, PCV20 was predicted to be the dominant vaccination strategy versus both comparators. PCV20 was also dominant versus PCV13 in 97.40% of probabilistic sensitivity analysis iterations and versus PCV15 in 85.70% of iterations.Conclusions: This cost-effectiveness analysis estimated that adoption of PCV20 into the Australian paediatric NIP would be dominant versus PCV13 and PCV15, leading to health benefits and cost-savings.

title: Nonlinear Environmental Impacts of Information Infrastructure: From Initial Pollution to Green Tech Gains
affiliations: Beijing Jiaotong University and Beijing Jiaotong University

detail.title: Nonlinear Environmental Impacts of Information Infrastructure: From Initial Pollution to Green Tech Gains
detail.abstract: This study assesses the environmental impacts of information infrastructure development, specifically analyzing its effect on air pollution indicators such as carbon emissions and PM2.5 levels. Initial findings indicate that while early stages of infrastructure development tend to increase pollution due to industrial expansion, the adoption of advanced, eco-friendly technologies eventually leads to notable environmental improvements. The research highlights significant regional differences; energy-exporting regions experience reduced pollution with infrastructure improvements, whereas energy-importing areas see immediate reductions in PM2.5 during initial stages. These strategies aim to harmonize infrastructure development with environmental sustainability objectives, providing a strategic framework for mitigating pollution while fostering technological advancement.

title: Multi-time Scale Optimal Dispatching of Integrated Energy in the Industrial Park Considering Green Certificate-carbon Collaborative Trading
affiliations: Yunnan Power Grid Co., Ltd., Yunnan Power Grid Co., Ltd., Yunnan Power Grid Co., Ltd., Yunnan Power Grid Co., Ltd., Yunnan Power Grid Co., Ltd. and Yunnan Power Grid Co., Ltd.

detail.title: Multi-time Scale Optimal Dispatching of Integrated Energy in the Industrial Park Considering Green Certificate-carbon Collaborative Trading
detail.abstract: Renewable energies have become the core driver of energy transition within industrial parks. However,their inherent uncertainties plus load fluctuation pose major challenges to the dispatch of integrated energy.Though carbon emission trading (CET) and green certificate trading (GCT) serve as key tools to curbexcessive energy use and emissions, thereby supporting energy transition, the coordinated optimization of their economic benefits and emission-reduction effects remains underexplored. This study proposes a multi-timescale optimal dispatching framework that integrates GCT-CET synergy and comprehensive demand response (DR), featuring a three-stage implementation scheme: day-ahead optimization, intra-day adjustment, and real-time correction. In the day-ahead scheduling phase, the GCT-CET collaborative trading and price-based DR are combined to optimize unit output and reduce carbon emissions. In the intra-day scheduling phase, incentive-based DR is used to further smooth load fluctuations. In the real-time scheduling phase, the deviation from the intra-day plan is corrected. Results demonstrate that day-ahead scheduling reduces total park costs by 4.2% and carbon emissions by 50.7%. Intra-day scheduling lowers contact line power fluctuation by 5.2%. Real-time scheduling corrects deviations, validating uncertainty mitigation. This multi-timescale optimization strategies enhances hybrid storage responsiveness, mitigates uncertainties, bridges gaps in standalone CET/GCT and fragmented DR, enriching industrial parks’economic-environmental optimization theories.

title: Walter Lippmann: A Proto-Public Choice Theorist
affiliations: Northwood University and Middle Tennessee State University - Department of Economics and Finance

detail.title: Walter Lippmann: A Proto-Public Choice Theorist

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: The authors received no dedicated funding for this project.

detail.abstract: This article explores Walter Lippmann’s intellectual contributions in light of public choice theory. We argue that Lippmann’s approach to politics challenges the common romantic views of his time by offering a pragmatic perspective in which politics is understood as an imperfect process, with unintended consequences and the self-interest of political actors playing a major role in creating the resulting order. Hence, Lippmann can be seen as a proto-public choice theorist, anticipating key insights later developed and formalized by James Buchanan, Gordon Tullock, and others. This perspective provides a framework to interpret the trajectory of Lippmann’s thinking on political economy.

title: Not Just Who Wins, But by How Much: Electoral Decisiveness and Market Outcomes
affiliations: University of Colorado at Denver - Department of Finance

detail.title: Not Just Who Wins, But by How Much: Electoral Decisiveness and Market Outcomes
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how the margin of victory (MoV) in U.S. presidential elections influences stock market outcomes. We hypothesize that a larger MoV makes households less averse to risk and more optimistic, thereby boosting returns. At the same time, a decisive victory reduces political and regulatory uncertainty, lowering market volatility. To address potential endogeneity, we exploit election-day weather shocks across the 50 largest U.S. cities as an instrumental variable. The effects of MoV vary across sectors and firm sizes, with the strongest impact on small-cap stocks. Results remain robust across political contexts, showing that markets respond not only to who wins, but also to the scale of their victory, reflecting investor confidence in the president's mandate.

title: The Microsoft Formula For Platform Power: Do Significant Network Effects Inevitably Generate Winnder-Takes-All Dynamics?
affiliations: University of Chicago - Law School and University of Haifa - Faculty of Law

detail.title: The Microsoft Formula For Platform Power: Do Significant Network Effects Inevitably Generate Winnder-Takes-All Dynamics?
detail.abstract:
• This article contests Microsoft's popular assertion that markets driven by significant network effects lead to a winner-takes-all outcome. Specifically, it disputes the doctrinal "Formula" for establishing monopoly power in platform markets that has stemmed from this assertion: that demonstrating the presence of network effects and substantial market share is sufficient to show that a platform incontrovertibly holds entrenched monopoly power.
• It explains that Microsoft's reasoning crystallized nascent economic theories regarding network effects into an actionable legal doctrine broadly applicable across diverse platform settings. Yet the mid-1980s scholarship that informed these theories forced pioneering economists to adopt simplifying assumptions in their models. • Since then, dramatic advances in network science have provided far more sophisticated analytical tools. Rudimentary theoretical abstractions have evolved into highly sophisticated computational models, bolstered by data-based empirical research. Accordingly, antitrust no longer needs to be confined by such overly simplistic assumptions.
• The article explores several blind spots in Microsoft's reasoning on network effects, acknowledging existing criticisms while highlighting newer insights drawn from network science's more advanced understanding of platform dynamics. • It then proposes an enhanced framework for evaluating the impact of network effects on a platform's market power-one that better integrates modern theory, methodological capabilities, and the goals of antitrust.

title: Estimating the Impact of the Pay-As-You-Throw Program on Waste Reduction: Using MTE Analysis
affiliations: , Yamanashi Eiwa College and

detail.title: Estimating the Impact of the Pay-As-You-Throw Program on Waste Reduction: Using MTE Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the waste reduction effect of the pay-as-you-throw (PAYT) program, which charges households for non-recyclable household waste, while accounting for self-selection into treatment. To address self-selection bias and heterogeneous treatment effects related to municipalities' willingness to adopt PAYT, we estimate the marginal treatment effect (MTE) using the fiscal condition of municipalities as an instrumental variable, since fiscally constrained municipalities tend to adopt PAYT even though residents' waste disposal behavior is not directly influenced by fiscal condition. By estimating the MTE, we find that PAYT promotes recycling and reduces household waste, but the magnitude of these effects depends on municipalities' adoption propensity. We also find that PAYT does not reduce total waste when business-related waste is considered, because PAYT induces immoral disposal: residents facing PAYT discard household waste as business-related waste at shops and firms with public trash cans.

title: Balancing Transparency in FinTech Regulatory Sandboxes: Best Practices for Financial Regulators Regarding Intellectual Property, Data Privacy, and Administrative Burden Mitigation
affiliations: Auckland Institute of Studies

detail.title: Balancing Transparency in FinTech Regulatory Sandboxes: Best Practices for Financial Regulators Regarding Intellectual Property, Data Privacy, and Administrative Burden Mitigation
detail.abstract: This research project investigates just how financial regulators are able to improve transparency in FinTech regulatory sandboxes as well as how they are able to safeguard intellectual property (IP), ensure data privacy, and reduce administrative burdens, a challenge conceptualised as the "transparency trilemma." Through a qualitative comparative case study of five jurisdictions: the United Kingdom, Singapore, Colombia, Kenya, and Canada, this study analyses sandbox frameworks right across common law and civil law traditions. Within each jurisdiction, transparency practices were assessed systematically by way of a novel Transparency Evaluation Rubric. Alongside this, a tiered disclosure model was also developed. Findings reveal that the UK and Singapore excel in transparency and data governance because of structured public reporting and strong IP and privacy protections, yet civil law jurisdictions like Colombia stress statutory control, frequently costing agility. In the meantime, Kenya and Canada strive for innovation, achieving rather mixed outcomes in terms of their transparency and their stakeholder engagement. Sandbox frameworks are important for reaching a dynamic balance among regulatory integrity, innovation, and transparency, being iterative, adaptive and rooted in context-specific legal and regulatory capabilities, the study concludes. The research contributes toward global financial governance discourse. As this research provides actionable recommendations and a functional assessment resource, regulators may nurture innovation without affecting key regulatory aims.

title: The Economic Gains from Renewable Energy: Evidence from China's Land Market
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE), Lanzhou University, Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE) - School of Economics, Business School, National University of Singapore, Lanzhou University and National University of Singapore

detail.title: The Economic Gains from Renewable Energy: Evidence from China's Land Market
detail.abstract: Renewable energy is widely recognized as an effective solution to environmental challenges, yet its economic benefits remain underexplored. Leveraging granular data on power plant installations and land transactions in China, we estimate the impacts of newly opened power plants across various energy types on land values using a difference-in-differences framework. The findings highlight the economic benefits of renewable energy. Introducing a coal-fired power plant reduces land prices within 1.5 km by 12.99%, whereas renewable power plants have no such negative effect. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the price discount from coal-fired power plants is particularly pronounced for non-industrial land parcels and those located in richer cities. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that transitioning to renewable energy infrastructure could yield land value gains of 9.56 billion RMB per year, accounting for 2.28‰ of annual total land revenues.

title: An Analysis of Agricultural Crop Residue Burning and Urban Air Pollution in New Delhi, India
affiliations: Rochester Institute of Technology and University of Texas at San Antonio - College of Business - Department of Economics

detail.title: An Analysis of Agricultural Crop Residue Burning and Urban Air Pollution in New Delhi, India
detail.abstract: A farmer in Haryana, a state neighboring the capital city of New Delhi, India, burns agricultural crop residue which leads to an increase in air pollution and gives rise to extra costs for a small business owning representative citizen in New Delhi. We theoretically analyze this farmer/citizen interaction. We first determine the optimal amount of crop produced when the farmer disregards the negative externality he imposes on the representative New Delhi citizen. Second, we study the equilibrium that emerges when the farmer must pay a fine to compensate the New Delhi citizen for the negative externality he causes. Finally, we compare the outcomes in the preceding two cases and then explain the differences that arise.

title: Assessing Dianov's "Harmonious Worldview": Demarcation, Method, and Misuse of Physics
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Assessing Dianov's "Harmonious Worldview": Demarcation, Method, and Misuse of Physics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal conflicts of interest that could have influenced the research, analysis, or conclusions of this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, animals, or case studies requiring ethical approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper critically evaluates Vyacheslav Dianov's Harmonious Worldview, a sixty-page essay that proposes a spiritual alternative to materialist science. While the text presents itself as a scientific framework, its claims fail to meet basic criteria of scientific inquiry. Drawing on Popper's principle of falsifiability and Kuhn's paradigm theory, I assess the work through textual analysis and a review of its frequently cited empirical references, including the "soul weight" hypothesis, torsion field theory, and Kirlian photography. The analysis demonstrates that Dianov's arguments are unfalsifiable, methodologically unsupported, and conceptually inconsistent, often conflating scientific concepts such as "energy" and "field" with metaphysical or spiritual meanings. Rather than constituting a viable scientific theory, Harmonious Worldview functions as a spiritual manifesto cloaked in scientific terminology. The critique situates this case within broader patterns of pseudoscientific discourse, in which the authority of physics is invoked rhetorically while its empirical standards are abandoned.

title: Removing Barriers to Investment, Competition, and Movement: A Historical Lesson
affiliations: George Mason University - Department of Economics and Mount Allison University

detail.title: Removing Barriers to Investment, Competition, and Movement: A Historical Lesson
detail.abstract: During the Canadian Wheat Boom (1896–1913), Canada experienced remarkable economic growth on both the intensive and extensive margins. Canada’s economic growth at this time outpaced most of the rest of the world, and was higher than Canada has ever seen before or since. In this policy report, we provide historical evidence suggesting that the “Wheat” Boom had less to do with wheat and agricultural exports, and more to do with a government allowing (and even encouraging) the free flow of foreign capital and labour into the country. Guided by this historical case study, we recommend that today’s policymakers re-embrace openness and remove artificial barriers to investment, competition, and movement (of both capital and labour), if their goal is to achieve more robust economic growth in Canada.

title: The Theory of Artificial Intelligence Innovation
affiliations: goldennanox and goldennanox

detail.title: The Theory of Artificial Intelligence Innovation
detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Theory of Artificial Intelligence Innovation, which systematically elaborates the fundamental laws of artificial intelligence in three aspects: knowledge acquisition, path exploration, and continuous innovation. The first law states that artificial intelligence has the potential ability to read, write, and understand the entirety of human knowledge, encompassing multimodal information such as literature, language, and video, thereby becoming a "hypothetical human" mastering all human knowledge. The second law emphasizes that artificial intelligence can discover and apply previously unknown rules and knowledge of the world by traversing possible paths and combining them with feedback verification, where the results are scored and optimized for validity. The third law asserts that the innovative capacity of artificial intelligence is theoretically unlimited, constrained only by computing power and storage; as innovation continues to expand, the demands for computation and storage will grow exponentially. This theory provides a foundational framework for understanding the knowledge boundaries, innovative potential, and future development trends of artificial intelligence, and offers new perspectives for its strategic deployment in scientific research, industrial applications, and social governance.

title: Abolishing the Color Line: W. E. B. Du Bois's Theory of Dynamic Social Equilibrium
affiliations: Department of Economics, Colorado State University, Fort Collins and

detail.title: Abolishing the Color Line: W. E. B. Du Bois's Theory of Dynamic Social Equilibrium
detail.abstract: This article explores the political economy of W. E. B. Du Bois drawing on the mathematical analogies and theoretical insights presented in "The Future of the Negro Race in America," a rarely discussed essay that examines the conditions for "the abolition of the colour line." The term expresses Du Bois's demand for "full rights and citizenship"–namely, "full and fair equality" for Black Americans. We argue that Du Bois put forward a dynamic model of social equilibrium that sheds brighter light on the factors that affect the socioeconomic advancement of Black Americans. The main feature of the model is the interdependence between the social condition of a marginalized group and public opinion. We develop a formal Du Boisian model that distinguishes between four regimes. A shock to education improves the social condition of the Black community. This will then affect public opinion, which in turn will change social conditions, and the process will continue until a new steady state is reached at a higher value of education. A shock to integration creates a similar process. Du Bois's framework is then compared with Gunnar Myrdal's model of dynamic causation. We contend that Du Bois should be considered a major theorist of social dynamics.

title: Constrained Optimization or Observation? On What Economists Take as Primary
affiliations: Chapman University - Smith Institute for Political Economy and Philosophy

detail.title: Constrained Optimization or Observation? On What Economists Take as Primary
detail.abstract: Economists differ on what they take as primary when constructing the problem of a rational economic order: constrained optimization or observation. The general starting point is to frame the problem with four key assumptions-scarcity, fixed preferences, complete information, and selfinterest-so that the optimization problem yields a clear prediction. Observation enters only after the fact, to repair the model when predictions fail. F. A. Hayek and Vernon Smith instead begin with what people actually know and do, making observation primary to economic inquiry. Humanomics extends this stance by grounding human conduct in Adam Smith's astute observations of fellow-feeling, moral sentiments, and a sense of propriety. Economics as an observational science takes human conduct, not constrained optimization, as primary.

reference: Journal of Business Venturing, volume 40, issue 6, 2025[10.1016/j.jbusvent.2025.106527]
title: Cognitive Origins of Entrepreneurial Action: How Venture-Specific Knowledge Drives Financial Investments
affiliations: Loyola University Chicago and Loyola University Chicago

detail.title: Cognitive Origins of Entrepreneurial Action: How Venture-Specific Knowledge Drives Financial Investments

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Business Venturing, volume 40, issue 6, 2025[10.1016/j.jbusvent.2025.106527]

detail.abstract:
Entrepreneurial action under uncertainty requires resource commitment, yet the cognitive mechanisms enabling such decisions remain underexplored.
This study investigates the role of venture-specific knowledge (VSK) in entrepreneurial action, focusing on two distinct cognitive pathways:
refinement, which enhances understanding to address ignorance, and conviction, which strengthens confidence to overcome doubt. Using a causal
map representation of VSK, we demonstrate that refinement and conviction independently drive personal financial investment, while also acting as
substitutes when one pathway reaches its limits. Our findings extend entrepreneurial action theory by highlighting the distinct cognitive processes
underlying VSK. Furthermore, we examine how these pathways interact with individual traits such as entrepreneurial self-efficacy (ESE) and uncertainty
avoidance, revealing nuanced moderating effects. These insights advance understanding of entrepreneurial decision making under irreducible
uncertainty and provide implications for both theory and practice.

title: Retaliatory Recognition: A New Paradigm in Diplomatic Recognition
affiliations: Harvard University - Harvard Law School

detail.title: Retaliatory Recognition: A New Paradigm in Diplomatic Recognition
detail.abstract: The belated recognition of Palestine by France, the UK, Canada, and Australia arguably represents a new paradigm of diplomatic recognition, one which could be described as “retaliatory recognition” or “offensive recognition.” Under this paradigm, the recognition of a country is not primarily based on the Montevideo Convention, or on the legitimacy or illegitimacy of the state’s formation, or even on a material change in political reality such as a declaration of independence. Instead, diplomatic recognition is used as an offensive tactic and a diplomatic rebuke against a third party, without the intention of breaking off ties with that third party altogether. This is quite a novel phenomenon in international relations that has rarely been encountered before, in part because relatively few countries have intentionally withheld recognition of a sovereign state on political grounds. Even when this has been the case, countries have been reluctant to shift their position in the absence of a change in the political reality, such as an overthrow of the old regime. Thus, it is possible that the world is entering a new era in which diplomatic recognition can be used to not only promote ties between two states but also to protest the behavior of a third party, which this party will analyze.

title: Systemic Financial Vulnerabilities and the Japanese Debt Crisis: An Empirical Analysis of Global Contagion Mechanisms in Bond Market Disruption
affiliations: Randolph College

detail.title: Systemic Financial Vulnerabilities and the Japanese Debt Crisis: An Empirical Analysis of Global Contagion Mechanisms in Bond Market Disruption

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author acknowledges valuable research assistance from the Bank of Japan's Financial Markets Department, the International Monetary Fund's Monetary and Financial Systems Department, the Bank for International Settlements' Monetary and Economic Department, the Federal Reserve Board's Division of Monetary Affairs, and the University of Michigan Survey Research Center. All errors remain the responsibility of the author.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was not supported by any entity through monetary assistance.

detail.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive empirical analysis of the escalating bond yield crisis centered in Japan and its potential to trigger a global financial system collapse through interconnected transmission mechanisms. Bond markets, often dismissed as the dull cousin of equities, have become a flashing red warning light signaling unprecedented systemic vulnerabilities. After more than a decade of historically low interest rates and aggressive central bank asset purchases, longterm government bond yields in major economies have surged beyond cyclical adjustment patterns to represent a fundamental structural shift toward potential financial catastrophe. Using novel Bank of Japan granular transaction data, International Monetary Fund debt sustainability frameworks, and Bank for International Settlements global liquidity indicators, we document how Japan's debt-to-GDP ratio of 260% combined with Bank of Japan balance sheet losses of 198 trillion creates conditions for what institutional analysts characterize as potential "global financial market Armageddon." Public debt has climbed to levels normally seen only after major wars, while economic growth and productivity remain muted. Central banks are unwinding massive holdings of government debt, pushing term premiums higher as the correlation between bond and stock returns has turned positive, eroding bonds' traditional portfolio hedge function. Through examination of $3.6 trillion in global carry trade exposures, cross-border banking flows exceeding $1.15 trillion in U.S. Treasury holdings alone, and deteriorating bond market liquidity metrics, we demonstrate how Japan's monetary policy normalization process has created multiple pathways for rapid contagion propagation across developed and emerging market economies. The research reveals a dangerous dissonance between speculative equity markets setting record highs and a strained real economy where households struggle with soaring credit-card balances, rising delinquencies, and falling consumer confidence. Our findings indicate that the structural unwinding of three decades of ultra-accommodative monetary policy represents not a cyclical adjustment but a fundamental regime shift with implications extending far beyond Japanese markets, requiring immediate coordinated international monetary policy responses to prevent cascading failures across interconnected global financial networks.

title: Beyond Border: How International Courts Address Human Rights Violations
affiliations: Symbiosis Centre of Distance Learning

detail.title: Beyond Border: How International Courts Address Human Rights Violations
detail.abstract: The concept of human rights transcends national boundaries. When widespread or systematic violations occur, the international community has a responsibility to intervene. This paper examines how international courts address human rights violations beyond borders. It explores the key institutions – the International Criminal Court (ICC), the International Court of Justice (ICJ), and regional human rights courts – and their respective mechanisms for investigating, prosecuting, and adjudicating human rights abuses. The paper analyses the impact of these courts in promoting accountability and deterring future violations. It also acknowledges the challenges these institutions face, including limitations on jurisdiction, enforcement issues, and concerns about selectivity. Finally, the paper proposes solutions to strengthen the effectiveness of international courts in upholding human rights globally, including universal ratification of the Rome Statute, enhanced cooperation and enforcement mechanisms, and addressing issues of bias. By holding perpetrators accountable and deterring future abuses, international courts play a vital role in ensuring the universality and respect for human rights beyond borders.

title: Supplanting or Supplementing: The Stickiness of Title I Revenues in Post-Adequacy Era

detail.title: Supplanting or Supplementing: The Stickiness of Title I Revenues in Post-Adequacy Era
detail.abstract: This paper examines how school districts respond to federal Title I funding in the post-adequacy era. Using a stacked regression discontinuity design, I find no systematic crowd-out of state or local operating revenue. Instead, a clear fiscal adjustment occurs through capital investment. Title I leads to a significant decrease in capital expenditures, driven by a reduction in bond elections. These results suggest that recent education finance reforms, while constraining traditional crowd-out, have redirected fiscal substitution toward less visible capital spending, highlighting the need for safeguards to protect long-term infrastructure investment.

title: Nowcasting and Backcasting Credit with Mixed-Frequency Data and Machine Learning: Evidence from Peru
affiliations: Central Reserve Bank of Peru and Unaffiliated Author

detail.title: Nowcasting and Backcasting Credit with Mixed-Frequency Data and Machine Learning: Evidence from Peru

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known com peting financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a real-time framework for nowcasting and backcasting credit growth in Peru by integrating mixed-frequency data with machine learning techniques. Using an unrestricted MIDAS (U-MIDAS) approach combined with penalized regression and forecast combination methods, we design a sequence of forecasts aligned with the actual information release calendar of the Central Bank of Peru. The framework exploits daily financial and macroeconomic indicators to compensate for the long publication lags of monthly credit statistics. Outof-sample results for 2023-2024 show that regularized linear models-particularly Lasso, Elastic Net, and their adaptive variants-deliver substantial gains relative to autoregressive benchmarks, reducing forecast errors by up to 35%. Forecast combination methods based on the Model Confidence Set (MCS) procedure yield the most stable and accurate improvements, consistently outperforming both benchmarks and nonlinear machine learning models. Variable-importance analysis highlights the central role of lagged credit, liquidity conditions, interest rate spreads, and reserve requirements, while also revealing how the relative weight of predictors shifts dynamically with the information flow. Overall, the findings suggest that credit dynamics in emerging markets remain largely linear and persistent, favoring transparent shrinkage-based models and disciplined forecast aggregation over more complex "black-box" approaches. From a policy perspective, the proposed framework provides a timely and interpretable tool for real-time credit surveillance, supporting more informed monetary and financial stability decisions.

title: Mediation Effect of Perceived Stress on the Relationship between Emotional Intelligence and Life Satisfaction Among Low-Income Adults in Selangor, Malaysia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM), Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM), Ministry of Health Malaysia - Botanic Health Clinic and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Mediation Effect of Perceived Stress on the Relationship between Emotional Intelligence and Life Satisfaction Among Low-Income Adults in Selangor, Malaysia
detail.abstract: Perceived stress is a key psychological factor affecting life satisfaction. While emotional intelligence has been associated with reduced stress and improved wellbeing, limited research has explored the mechanism linking emotional intelligence to life satisfaction in low-income groups. This study examined whether perceived stress mediates the relationship between emotional intelligence and life satisfaction among low-income adults in Malaysia. A cross-sectional study was conducted with 427 participants recruited through convenience sampling from a primary healthcare clinic. Eligible participants were Malaysian citizens, literate in Malay, and eligible for the PeKa B40 scheme. Individuals with psychiatric disorders, physical disabilities, or cognitive impairments were excluded. The required sample size was calculated based on guidelines for mediation analysis with bootstrapping, adjusted for non-response. Validated Malay versions of questionnaires were administered. Mediation analysis was performed using the PROCESS Macro, controlling for age and ethnicity. Results showed that emotional intelligence was negatively associated with perceived stress (β = -0.12, p < .001), which in turn negatively predicted life satisfaction (β = -0.19, p < .001). Perceived stress partially mediated this relationship (β = 0.03, 95% CI: 0.01–0.03). These findings highlight the importance of emotional intelligence as a protective psychological resource in enhancing wellbeing among low-income adults.

title: The Convergence Against Homeplace

detail.title: The Convergence Against Homeplace
detail.abstract:
The public education and family regulation systems converge in ways that many scholars and policymakers have yet to fully confront. Although these systems claim to protect the interests of children and families, they often operate together in ways that disproportionately harm racially minoritized communities. This convergence undermines “homeplace,” the site where families construct mutual affirmation, resist caste-based hierarchies, and nurture autonomy. Extending bell hooks’s theory of homeplace into legal discourse, this Article argues that protecting homeplace requires understanding its historical significance and the structural forces that continue to threaten it.

Using homeplace as a critical lens, the Article traces how education and family regulation systems converge to produce overlapping harms, including excessive surveillance, punishment, legal estrangement, and civic disillusionment. These harms expose the dangers of state protection and the fragility of democratic legitimacy when broad swaths of entire communities are alienated from legal and educational institutions. The Article offers homeplace as both an interpretive framework for understanding systemic harm and a guide for imagining more liberatory, community-centered approaches. It assesses the possibilities and limitations of rights-based, regulatory, and grassroots strategies to reclaim homeplace and reimagine the state’s role in the lives of families.

title: Artificial Intelligence, CEO Turnover, and Exploration Orientation in Firm Innovation
affiliations: Marshall School of Business - University of Southern California, University of Pennsylvania and University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, CEO Turnover, and Exploration Orientation in Firm Innovation

declarations.funderStatement: The authors acknowledge generous research support from the Mack Institute Research Fellowship and Analytics at Wharton.

detail.abstract: This study examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in facilitating corporate innovation following a CEO turnover event. Using patent and job posting data, we find that firms with greater AI investment, as measured in hiring of employees with AI skills, are more successful in explorative innovation after CEO turnover events. Further analyses show that this effect is likely due to the firms with AI investment being better positioned to enable strategic change in innovation by (1) improving resource allocation to R&D investment, (2) prioritizing innovation as a central element of the firm's strategic vision, and (3) driving the operational implementation of innovation through new initiatives. Importantly, AI enables strategic change in part by mitigating myopic management and overcoming information overload that new CEOs often encounter. Overall, this study highlights the strategic value of AI in promoting exploration in innovation during organizational transition periods, offering insights into leveraging AI for transformation and creativity when navigating dynamic environments.

title: Meaning in Communication Games *
affiliations: University of Arizona - Department of Economics

detail.title: Meaning in Communication Games *
detail.abstract: I explore the role of a pre-existing language in strategic communication. A sender-receiver game combined with a language, modeled as a pure receiver strategy, is a language game. The sender deliberates by iterating pure-strategy best replies, starting from the language, while provisionally dropping unused messages. This process converges to a limit set of strategies in a reduced game. A minimal enlargement of this limit set contains a best reply to every belief concentrated on it, and hence supports an equilibrium of the reduced game. With a common language this equilibrium can be extended to the entire game by restoring dropped messages and is then a language equilibrium. The paper proposes a generalization to games with language uncertainty. Every finite language game has a language equilibrium, which predicts language use.

title: Cost Pass-Through Across Multiproduct Firms: Edgeworth's Paradox in Monopoly, Oligopoly, and Perfect Competition
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Korea University and Humboldt University of Berlin - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Cost Pass-Through Across Multiproduct Firms: Edgeworth's Paradox in Monopoly, Oligopoly, and Perfect Competition
detail.abstract: The literature on Edgeworth's paradox focused on monopoly and assumed symmetry of the Jacobian matrix of inverse demand functions. We relax the symmetry assumption and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the paradox to occur in monopoly, oligopoly, and perfect competition. Major new results hinge upon assuming that firms compete, together with asymmetries of the Jacobian of inverse demand. Under these conditions an increased cost of one good may not only lower the prices of all goods, but also increase the aggregate output of the good whose cost has increased-a "double" Edgeworth paradox inconceivable in monopoly.

title: Geopolitical Risk and IPO Outcomes
affiliations: University of Birmingham, Bayes Business School, City, University of London and University of Bath - School of Management

detail.title: Geopolitical Risk and IPO Outcomes
detail.abstract: We find that heightened geopolitical risk increases listing costs and reduces IPO activity. Issues launched during high-risk periods are more underpriced, though this effect is attenuated by reduced information asymmetry, regulatory reforms, and external governance mechanisms. Such issues also experience downward price revisions, smaller offer sizes, lower free floats, and weaker subscription levels. Moreover, they display stronger disclosure practices, pay higher underwriter fees, and are more likely to employ underwriter syndicates. These findings are robust to alternative measures of geopolitical risk and IPO activity, across sub-samples, and under different econometric specifications. Our evidence highlights the role of geopolitical risk in shaping global IPO pricing and structure, investor sentiment, and the risktaking incentives of intermediaries.

title: Pro-Competition Regulation: Lessons from the Telecoms Sector for Digital Platforms.
affiliations: London School of Economics and Independent

detail.title: Pro-Competition Regulation: Lessons from the Telecoms Sector for Digital Platforms.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: This paper addresses different ways of addressing the control of market power by major global digital platforms. It does so by comparing the approach taken in the USA, which involves reliance on competition law (including breakups), and the approach in the European Union, where sector-specific legislation in the form of the 2022 Digital Markets Act is employed,. The question is framed as a choice between competition law and a mode of pro-competition regulation in the form of mandated sharing, which requires the dominant firm to share some of its assets with competitors. The assumed goals of the process are to protect direct customers of the dominant firm, and to prevent it from extending its power up or down the value chain (or ecosystem) by self-preference. The main discussion is preceded by a comparison of the parallel case of telecommunications in the period from 1980, comparing the USA's breakup strategy with EU's mandated sharing or unbundling one. The paper then examines the competition law cases currently in progress in the USA, which, if proven, may use breakup or equivalent as a chief remedy. While recognising the uncertainties of the current situation, it suggests that this approach will be protracted, incomplete, and of uncertain outcome. It argues that in the EU a combination of the institutional framework for enforcement and mandated sharing or interoperability available under the DMA is likely to be more productive in achieving the stated objectives.

title: State Space Hedonic Models: Application to the Market for Female Surrealist Painters
affiliations: ArtMetrica

detail.title: State Space Hedonic Models: Application to the Market for Female Surrealist Painters
detail.abstract: This paper introduces State Space Hedonic Models (SSHM), reconceptualizing price evolution as a continuous latent process updated with each transaction, thereby addressing fundamental limitations in traditional Time Dummy Hedonic Models that prove particularly problematic in sparse data environments: artificial calendar aggregation, heterogeneous estimation precision, and outlier sensitivity. We establish formal variance dominance results proving SSHM's superiority. Empirical application to Female Surrealists demonstrates substantial methodological advantages, with return volatility estimates reduced tenfold, while revealing stylised facts about this art movement: 6% compound annual growth over 1985-2025, with artists typically peaking after 40 years of secondary market activity at 30-fold initial valuations.

title: Monetary Variables, Economic Growth and Monetary Policy in Nigeria
affiliations: Bayero University Kano - Department of Economics, Federal University of Kashere,  Kashere, Gombe State, Nigeria, Kebbi State Polytechnic - Department of Social Sciences, Federal University of Kashere,  Kashere, Gombe State, Nigeria and Federal University of Kashere,  Kashere, Gombe State, Nigeria

detail.title: Monetary Variables, Economic Growth and Monetary Policy in Nigeria
detail.abstract: Historically, monetary policy in Nigeria has been dominated by short term considerations. In the past few decades, monetary policy has bounced between short term and medium term considerations. Nigerian government might have tried to ensure some effectiveness in regulatory and supervisory mechanism of the entire monetary and financial ecosystem. This paper measures the influence of monetary variables on economic growth in Nigeria. Subsequently, it tests money demand function in Nigeria. It employs Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) and Autoregressive Distributed Lag Model (ARDL) for the analysis, using annual data from 1989 to 2019. The results of the analysis show money supply (M2) as important in explaining economic growth in Nigeria. The result also shows negative effects of Nigerian foreign exchange policy on economic growth in Nigeria. The result of the money demand analysis shows that income is the most important variable that explains money demand in Nigeria, even more important than interest rate which shows insignificant result. The paper recommends changes in Nigerian foreign exchange policy as the existing policies (especially, the policy somersault) are detrimental to economic growth. The paper also noted the importance of making money supply (M2) to be in tandem with overall economic growth agenda.

title: Foreign Loans and Its Impact on Commercial Sovereignty
affiliations: Afe Babalola University

detail.title: Foreign Loans and Its Impact on Commercial Sovereignty
detail.abstract: Sovereignty is an important characteristic of a state. It provides the state the power to make independent decisions that protect its personal interest. In relation to commercial activities, Commercial Sovereignty governs the independence a country has in carry out its commercial decisions. In an economic environment, every country has the right to implement its commercial decisions and strategies free from hinderance and infringement from any outside institutions. However, with focus on Nigeria, the increasing level of its foreign loan and its external debt leaves it in such a position where it is at the mercy of its creditors. This study explores the concept of foreign loans and commercial sovereignty with focus of the impact the Latter has on the other. This research was conducted with the use of non-doctrinal methodology making use of data and responses collected through a survey for this research paper. The findings of this study suggest that there is a direct link between the foreign loans of Nigeria and its commercial sovereignty. Institutions like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank typically attach loan conditions that prioritize creditor interests over local development goals. As a result, Nigeria is frequently forced to shape its economic policies around loan repayments which reduces its selfreliance. Despite the fact that foreign loans and external borrowing may prove to be necessary in certain instances, this study shows the negative aspects of constant borrowing from foreign institutions as well as the reality Nigeria faces with a projected external debt service bill of $5.2 billion this year. This study concludes its research by providing recommendations to help Nigeria identify the multifaceted ways it could reduce its debt burden and secure its commercial sovereignty, these recommendations include but are not limited to; Investment in Export-Driven Sectors, Industrialization, Reduction of Government Spending etc.

title: Economic Growth and International Trade: A Symbiotic Relationship Explored through Economics and Law
affiliations: Manav Rachna University

detail.title: Economic Growth and International Trade: A Symbiotic Relationship Explored through Economics and Law
detail.abstract: Economic growth and international trade are intrinsically linked, forming a symbiotic relationship that is crucial for the prosperity of nations. This paper investigates the multifaceted connections between economic growth and international trade, analysing them through the lenses of both economics and law. By exploring this relationship, the study aims to elucidate how trade policies and legal frameworks can foster sustainable economic growth. From an economic perspective, international trade stimulates growth by allowing countries to specialize in the production of goods and services in which they have a comparative advantage. This specialization leads to increased efficiency, higher productivity, and the optimal allocation of resources, thereby boosting economic output and growth. Furthermore, trade exposes domestic industries to global competition, driving innovation, enhancing product quality, and reducing prices for consumers. Legally, international trade is governed by a complex web of agreements, regulations, and institutions designed to facilitate fair and equitable trade practices. This paper examines key legal frameworks, such as the World Trade Organization (WTO) agreements, bilateral and multilateral trade treaties, and national trade laws. It highlights how these legal instruments provide the necessary infrastructure for international trade, ensuring stability, predictability, and dispute resolution mechanisms that are essential for economic growth. The interplay between economics and law in the context of international trade is also scrutinized. The paper explores how economic theories inform trade policies and how legal frameworks can be adapted to respond to evolving economic realities. Additionally, it discusses the challenges and opportunities posed by globalization, technological advancements, and shifting geopolitical landscapes on the economic growth-trade nexus. Through a comprehensive analysis, this paper underscores the importance of coherent and synergistic economic and legal strategies in promoting international trade and sustaining economic growth. It advocates for policies that not only liberalize trade but also address concerns related to equity, environmental sustainability, and social inclusion, ensuring that the benefits of trade are broadly shared.

title: Evaluating RA 9003: A Student Critique about Solid Waste Management Act of 2000
affiliations: Independent and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Evaluating RA 9003: A Student Critique about Solid Waste Management Act of 2000
detail.abstract: This Critic paper contains all about the RA 9003 also known as Ecological Solid Waste Management Act 2000. It evaluates about its effectivity and ineffectivity to our country.

title: Political Alignment Shocks and Economic Policy Uncertainty: Evidence from U.S. States
affiliations: Sejong University,  and Sungkyunkwan University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Political Alignment Shocks and Economic Policy Uncertainty: Evidence from U.S. States
detail.abstract: Although policy uncertainty influences economic outcomes such as investment and consumption, its sources remain underexplored. We examine how political alignment between the president and state governors affects economic policy uncertainty. When the two are politically unaligned, divergent policy preferences can undermine coordination and reduce the predictability of which policies will prevail. We use monthly state-level data from 1985 to 2004 that combine the Economic Policy Uncertainty index of Baker, Davis, and Levy (2022) with gubernatorial election data. Using a regression discontinuity-based event study, we find that political alignment leads to a substantial short-term reduction in policy uncertainty.

title: The Value of Local Knowledge in Service Work
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics, Renmin University of China, Renmin University of China and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: The Value of Local Knowledge in Service Work
detail.abstract: Many service tasks appear mechanical, yet automating them can destroy value. We study this puzzle through the lens of local knowledge-the contextual, real-time information that workers gather through direct observation and interaction. A large restaurant chain experienced an unexpected system failure, forcing its outlets to switch from digital ordering to full human service. We leverage this natural experiment to examine how servers use two types of local knowledge that automated systems cannot easily access: real-time customer characteristics and product knowledge that allows credible, tailored recommendations. We find that human servers increase revenue per order by 6.5% compared to digital systems. These gains come from strategic use of local knowledge: they promote signature and high-margin items, and adjust strategies to context-recommending premium dishes to small groups, expanding quantities for larger groups, scaling back upselling during busy periods, and generating greater revenue in tourist areas where customers are less familiar with the menu. Our findings show that decentralized decision-making based on local knowledge creates value that centralized automated systems cannot match.

title: Inflation, Monetary Policy, and Capital-Labor Inequality
affiliations: University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics

detail.title: Inflation, Monetary Policy, and Capital-Labor Inequality

keywords: Income Distribution between Capital and Labor

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper estimates a New Keynesian model with heterogeneous agents to study the interactions among monetary policy, macroeconomic shocks, and the distribution of income between capital and labor. The model assumes two types of households: workers, who supply labor to firms and receive wage income, and capitalists, who own the firms and enjoy the corresponding profits. There are nominal rigidities in both the goods and labor markets. The structural model is estimated using Bayesian methods to match U.S. data on consumption, corporate profits, wages, inflation, and nominal interest rates, on a sample spanning more than six decades. The empirical results show that contractionary monetary policy and inflationary pricemarkup shocks lead to increases in inequality. Negative wage markup shocks, which proxy for declining workers’ bargaining power, are major drivers of peaks in inequality over the sample; together with price markup shocks, they also account for a significant share of the changes in inequality after COVID.

title: International Sanctions and Corruption
affiliations: University of Hamburg - Institute of Law and Economics, University of Trier - Faculty of Economics and University of Trier - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: International Sanctions and Corruption
detail.abstract: A major concern about the imposition of international sanctions is that they may permanently deteriorate the quality of institutions in target countries, potentially causing an increase in corruption. While case studies suggest that this is frequently the case, systematic evidence is so far missing. We provide the first cross-country statistical analysis of the impact of sanctions on public-sector corruption. Using a panel difference-in-differences model and an event study approach, we analyze sanctions against 125 countries from 1971 to 2019. Our results show that Western (and UN) sanctions cause a significant decline of corruption in democracies, while non-Western sanctions and those targeting autocracies have no systematic impact. Event study estimates time the reductions in corruption at about three to four years into the sanctions episode. They persist throughout the sanctions period, but once sanctions are lifted, corruption levels revert to their pre-treatment baseline, indicating that the corruption-reducing effect is limited to the duration of the sanctions episode. Further analysis reveals that the effect is stronger when sanctions explicitly target democratization or human rights improvements.

title: Dispute Resolution in Not-for-Profit Organizations: A Canadian Perspective
affiliations: Centre for the Study of Minority Cultures & Law

detail.title: Dispute Resolution in Not-for-Profit Organizations: A Canadian Perspective

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Conflucts
declarations.funderStatement: No funder

detail.abstract: This article explores dispute resolution practices within Canadian not-for-profit organizations, an essential but under-examined facet of nonprofit governance. With over 200,000 charities and nonprofits operating across Canada, conflicts in governance, personnel, and stakeholder relations are inevitable and potentially harmful. This study identifies common sources of disputes, analyzes the legal and regulatory context-including fiduciary duties and statutory remedies-and critiques the lack of sectorwide mechanisms to address conflict. Drawing on comparative examples from the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia, the article argues that Canada lacks a coherent infrastructure for nonprofit conflict resolution. Proposals include legislative amendments, improved bylaws, sector-wide mediation services, board education, and capacity building. The article contributes to nonprofit governance literature by offering a detailed roadmap for reform and emphasizing the importance of mission-aligned, accessible dispute resolution tools for a healthy civil society.

title: Transitology (1000-Word Entry from the Encyclopedia of Political Behavior)
affiliations: The University of Manchester - School of Law

detail.title: Transitology (1000-Word Entry from the Encyclopedia of Political Behavior)
detail.abstract: Transitology refers to the economic and socio-political reform efforts by Western governance to transform non-democratic states, and particularly the former Soviet Union, into a model premised on free-market principles and the rule of law. As a description and set of policy reforms, transitology is constituted on specific ideas about human behavior, societal characteristics and government functions. Though many of its core tenets continue to be popular within governance, it is widely seen as a policy failure in its historical contexts. This entry briefly introduces transitology literature as it relates to the former Soviet Union concerning economic debates and socio-political theory. The entry concludes with a concise discussion of how recent scholarship engages the legacy of transitology in contemporary governance.

title: Privilege, Path Dependence, and Development: The Long-Term Economic Impact of Institutional Discrimination in Historic Transylvania Research Paper
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Privilege, Path Dependence, and Development: The Long-Term Economic Impact of Institutional Discrimination in Historic Transylvania Research Paper
detail.abstract: This study examines the long-term economic consequences of institutional discrimination through an analysis of the formal exclusion of the Romanian majority from Transylvania's feudal institutions between 1366-1437. Using path dependence theory as a theoretical framework, we investigate whether this historical exclusion created persistent trajectories of institutional underdevelopment and economic inequality that continue to influence the region's socioeconomic structure today. Our empirical analysis employs county-level data across Romania, comparing Transylvanian counties to other historical regions using regression models that control for contemporary socioeconomic factors. The results indicate that counties in historical Transylvania exhibit significantly lower GDP per capita (€2,150 less on average) and higher income inequality (3.5 percentage points higher Gini coefficient) compared to other Romanian regions. These findings provide robust empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis that medieval institutional exclusion created path-dependent trajectories that continue to shape economic outcomes seven centuries later. The study contributes to the broader literature on institutional economics, historical determinants of development, and the persistence of inequality, while offering insights into how privilege structures can become embedded in regional economic systems across centuries.

title: Accusing and Believing in Equilibrium: Evidence from #MeToo
affiliations: and Brown University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Accusing and Believing in Equilibrium: Evidence from #MeToo
detail.abstract: Many social movements encourage reporting of wrongdoing, but critics argue this increases false accusations. We study how #MeToo-a social movement that encouraged reporting of sexual harassment-changed the truthfulness of sexual harassment accusations and adjudicators' willingness to believe them. We estimate that #MeToo increased the probability of winning a sexual harassment complaint by 10.1 pp. This increase can reflect stronger complaints filed (selection) or more favorable adjudicators (direct treatment). We develop a framework to separate these effects and find evidence for both channels. Exploiting complaints filed before but resolved after #MeToo to estimate the direct treatment effect, we show that adjudicators became more likely to rule in favor of complainants, particularly male complainants. Newly induced complaints became more likely to be substantiated, with women's complaints positively selected (more credible) and men's negatively selected (less credible).

title: Sanctions and Sanctions-Resistant Money
affiliations: University of Mississippi and Northern Illinois University

detail.title: Sanctions and Sanctions-Resistant Money
detail.abstract: In recent years, dollar-based sanctions have become an important tool of U.S. foreign policy. The introduction of bitcoin poses challenges to this sanctions regime. Bitcoin settles transactions through a decentralized, global, permissionless, and competitive market. These characteristics create a degree of censorship resistance. As bitcoin adoption increases, policymakers intent on maintaining the status quo might try to target the bitcoin network for censorship as well. We examine two recent proposals aimed at censoring transactions involving sanctioned entities and assesses their likelihood of success. We argue that both proposals are unlikely to achieve their intended outcomes. Instead, a more pragmatic approach to bitcoin is likely to be more effective for those focused on sanctions compliance and enforcement.

title: Detecting Structural Breaks in Oil Futures using MIDAS-ARDL Models
affiliations: , University of California Santa Barbara, University of Reading - ICMA Centre and University of Reading - ICMA Centre

detail.title: Detecting Structural Breaks in Oil Futures using MIDAS-ARDL Models
detail.abstract: Structural breaks and anomalies in time series regressions, particularly within autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) models, where covariates or factors are observed at different sampling time scales, introduce a novel challenge in time series modeling. In this paper, we propose a methodology to detect structural changes in the MIDAS-ARDL time series regression model. This model is particularly useful when the response series is recorded at a different frequency from the covariates, which themselves may vary in sampling frequencies. The structural change detection method is based on the Cross-Entropy approach, a fast and efficient algorithm to learn a distribution of potential structural breaks. We adapt this method into a Sequential Binary Segmentation process, resulting in the development of the SBS-CE algorithm. This allows for the detection of structural breaks across different model components, including the long-term trend, autoregressive coefficients, noise volatility, or the MIDAS regression structure. To demonstrate the application of the proposed methodology, we analyze the dynamics of West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude oil futures prices, which are regressed against several potential drivers of oil price dynamics. By applying the SBS-CE algorithm, we identify significant structural changes, including shocks in the oil return dynamics, with noticeable breaks in both mean and volatility. Additionally, we investigate the effects of various explanatory factors, such as the dollar index and energy indices, within the MIDAS framework, highlighting their influence on the oil futures price behavior.

title: Beyond the Taylor Rule
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance, University of California, Berkeley and Columbia University

detail.title: Beyond the Taylor Rule

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The Federal Reserve partially "looked through" the post-Covid rise in inflation and ultimately managed to bring about an "immaculate disinflation." The Fed's policy deviated strongly from the Taylor rule during this period. More generally, central banks with strong inflation-fighting credentials looked through post-Covid inflationary shocks yet experienced less inflation than more hawkish but less credible central banks. In light of this episode, we assess the degree to which the Taylor rule is descriptive, and the degree to which it should be viewed as prescriptive. While the Taylor rule (generally) fits well during the Greenspan period, it (generally) fits poorly in the early 1980s and after the early 2000s. Academic work has emphasized the role of the Taylor rule in preventing self-fulfilling fluctuations (guaranteeing determinacy). These concerns can be addressed with a shock-contingent commitment and are fragile to deviations from fully rational expectations. We discuss three reasons why optimal policy may not always imply a one-for-one response of interest rates to inflation (forward guidance, correlated shocks, and "long and variable lags"). The main challenge arising from such policies is not indeterminacy but erosion of inflation-fighting credibility and potential deanchoring of long-run inflation expectations. Only central banks with strongly anchored inflation expectations and large amounts of inflation-fighting credibility are likely to be able to look through inflationary shocks.

title: Inflation is Coming Back: China's Growth Challenges and Policy Endogeneity

detail.abstract: Inflation is Coming Back: China's Growth Challenges and Policy Endogeneity, September 9, 2012, on Sina Finance, elaborated on the many factors that led to a high probability of economic growth slowing down to 6-7% over the next decade. It reasoned China's going to endogenously prolong the infrastructure saturation process. title: Flexible Monitoring, Double Moral Hazard, and Fixed-Wage Contracts
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen (CUHK-Shenzhen), University of Amsterdam and UCL

detail.title: Flexible Monitoring, Double Moral Hazard, and Fixed-Wage Contracts
detail.abstract: A principal ("she") monitors an agent's("his") hidden action by allocating attention to observe his performance publicly; however, her own attention allocation is also her hidden action that she cannot commit to, leading to a double moral hazard problem. We study this problem in an infinite-horizon model where the principal can commit to the compensation scheme to varying degrees, but not to the monitoring scheme. We show that the optimal contract is a fixed wage paired with termination upon publicly observed bad performance, regardless of the degree of commitment in compensation. Introducing a minimal commitment to monitoring yields a more efficient contract by rewarding publicly observed good performance, thereby strengthening the agent's incentives, lowering his continuation value, and improving the principal's payoff. These findings offer a novel perspective on the prevalence of fixed-wage contracts in practice and how it may relate to limited commitment power in monitoring.

title: Are Financial Markets Good Predictors of R‑Star?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Federal Reserve Bank of New York

detail.title: Are Financial Markets Good Predictors of R‑Star?

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Recently, there has been renewed attention on the natural rate of interest—often referred to as “r-star”—and whether it has risen from the historically low levels that prevailed before the COVID-19 pandemic. The natural interest rate is the real (inflation-adjusted) interest rate expected to prevail when supply and demand in the economy are in balance and inflation is stable. Some commentators claim that the prior decline in r‑star has reversed, pointing to the recent rise in future real interest rates implied by the bond market. But before declaring the death of this “low r‑star” era, a natural question to ask is: how reliable are market-based measures of r‑star? In this Liberty Street Economics post, we evaluate whether such measures provide additional information on future real interest rates beyond what is already contained in macroeconomic model-based estimates of r-star. Our findings suggest they do not, and we conclude that reports of the death of low r-star are greatly exaggerated.

To view post:  https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2025/08/are-financial-markets-good-predictors-of-r-star/

title: Should Charitable and Political Donations Benefit from Similar Tax Treatments? Evidence from a Survey Experiment
affiliations: Sciences Po Paris Department of Economics, University of Liège and Paris School of Economics (PSE)

detail.title: Should Charitable and Political Donations Benefit from Similar Tax Treatments? Evidence from a Survey Experiment
detail.abstract: In many countries, both charitable and political donations benefit from generous-and often similar-tax incentives. While a large literature has studied the tax-price elasticity of charitable giving, little is known on political donations. Using a large-scale survey experiment (N = 12, 600), we investigate the relative efficiency of different tax schemes, and document that repealing the existing non refundable income-tax credit decreases charitable donations but not political donations, pointing toward more fiscal incentives behind charitable giving. Finally, we show that matching increases the amount received by both political parties and charities.

title: Firm Ownership and Pollution
affiliations: , Uppsala University and University of Pennsylvania - Business & Public Policy Department

detail.title: Firm Ownership and Pollution

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We provide a theoretical micro foundation for how much pollution (negative externalities) a firm will internalize based on the ownership distribution of its shareholders. Small shareholders, compared to large ones, want the firm to spend more on avoiding pollution since they suffer less profit loss for the same environmental benefit. In particular, if a shareholder holds a share of 1/N, where N is the population in society, that shareholder's preferences align with a social planner's. Three theoretical predictions arise. First, small shareholders will systematically vote for a greener corporate profile. Second, firms with a smaller weighted median shareholder will pollute less. Third, countries with concentrated corporate wealth holdings and/or more individualized firm ownership pollute more. This implies that standard models of externalities in environmental economics and macroeconomics containing representative agents are either internally inconsistent or not fully specified.

title: Long-run Uncovered Interest Parity in Emerging Markets
affiliations: , Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School and Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR)

detail.title: Long-run Uncovered Interest Parity in Emerging Markets
