title: Did BP Pay a Reputational Penalty for the Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill?
affiliations: Utrecht University - School of Economics

detail.title: Did BP Pay a Reputational Penalty for the Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Faure, M., Schreuders, W., & Visscher, L. T. (Eds.) (2018). Don't take it seriously. Essays in law and economics in honour of Roger Van den Bergh. Intersentia.

detail.abstract: In 2010 the British multinational oil and gas company BP was involved in an oil spill incident in the Gulf of Mexico following a fire on the Deepwater Horizon drilling platform BP lost no less than one third of its market value between the time of the start and the closing of the leak. This study analyzes whether BP’s stock market loss is due to reputational penalties for this environmental violation or whether it can be explained by expected clean-up costs and expected legal penalties.

title: Shareholder-connected Director Appointments: Evidence from Cross-ownership
affiliations: Grenoble Ecole de Management and Free University of Bolzano-Bozen

detail.title: Shareholder-connected Director Appointments: Evidence from Cross-ownership

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: We explore how cross-ownership affects non-executive director appointments. Using investor cross-ownership to proxy candidate connections to shareholders, we analyze 18,371 appointed directors against a pool of 329,521 potential counterfactual candidates. Our findings show a positive link between shareholder connections and director appointments. Firms with governance concerns tend to appoint connected directors, which shareholders perceive favorably, leading to improved stock returns and voting support. These appointments improve corporate governance and increase capital expenditures. Directors benefit from increased external job prospects and higher internal compensation.

title: The Africonomics Theory of Structural Justice: A Transformative Framework for Civilized and Prosperous Society
affiliations: Afrindependent Institute

detail.title: The Africonomics Theory of Structural Justice: A Transformative Framework for Civilized and Prosperous Society
detail.abstract: This paper presents the Africonomics Theory of Structural Justice (ATSJ), a core pillar in the broader Africonomics framework. It establishes the moral and institutional principles necessary to form a fundamentally ethical and structurally just socioeconomic order. Contrary to prevailing models—rooted in utilitarianism, positivism, and statism—Africonomics asserts that justice is not the product of electoral formalities or bureaucratic design, but of a system’s fidelity to objective moral principles and natural rights. The theory defines structural justice as the ethical alignment of legal and institutional foundations with natural-moral law and the individual rights to life, liberty, and property ownership. A structurally just system eliminates or minimizes institutionalized rights violations and prohibits aggression, fraud, and coercion—whether through state policies, monetary manipulation, or economic centralization. This paper reveals the inadequacy of modern democracy, exposes the failures of statist socioeconomic models, and outlines the principles, components, and institutional reforms required to build free, civilized, and prosperous societies.

title: Effects of Representativeness Bias on Investment Decisions of Selected Small and Medium Enterprises in Nairobi County
affiliations: Kisii University, Kisii University and Kisii University

detail.title: Effects of Representativeness Bias on Investment Decisions of Selected Small and Medium Enterprises in Nairobi County
detail.abstract: Investment decisions are significantly affected by behavioral biases, potentially leading to suboptimal financial outcomes. Investment decision-making in small and medium firms is frequently affected by cognitive biases, especially representativeness bias, causing investors to depend on perceived resemblances to prior experiences instead of objective evaluation. Comprehending the effects of this bias is essential for optimizing resource distribution, improving financial resilience, and guiding measures that foster rational investment decisions. This study examined the effect of representativeness bias on investment decisions of selected small and medium enterprises in Nairobi County. Grounded on Behavioral Portfolio Theory, and Heuristics Theory, this study employed a positivist research philosophy utilizing a cross-sectional and survey research design. A proportionate stratified random sampling was used to select a sample of 426 from 18,872 small and medium firms registered with the Micro and Small Enterprise Authority. Data was collected from 376 proprietors and managers of small and medium enterprises and analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics. Pearson correlation analysis revealed a weak statistically significant positive association between representativeness bias and investment decisions (r = 0.149, p = 0.004). Regression analysis results also showed that representativeness bias exerted a significant positive influence on investment decisions (β = 0.205, p = 0.004), accounting for 2.2% of the variance. From the study results, this study recommends that small and medium-sized enterprises should implement systematic investment strategies. Also, the Government of Kenya and financial institutions should establish financial literacy initiatives and decision-support frameworks to enhance objective investment analysis.

title: Confidential Bank Supervision in America: Historical Tensions and Modern Pressures
affiliations: Yale University

detail.title: Confidential Bank Supervision in America: Historical Tensions and Modern Pressures
detail.abstract: U.S. bank supervision relies on secrecy rules designed for a world that no longer exists. Confidentiality norms established in the nineteenth century, when banks were small, local institutions with simple balance sheets and few public reporting requirements, now apply to large publicly traded bank conglomerates that operate across global markets and face layers of disclosure. What started as a tool to prevent bank runs and encourage candid dialogue between regulators and banks has, over time, become entrenched and overextended within a far more complex financial system. Today, "Confidential Supervisory Information" ("CSI") encompasses a broad scope of information, including supervisory ratings, examination reports, informal supervisory guidance, and other regulatory communications, and is protected by regulators under statutes that carry potential criminal penalties. This paper reviews the history of bank supervision and CSI, examines the current challenges facing the CSI regime, illustrates tensions through case studies, and considers several areas of reform.

title: On the Conditions for Utilitarian Collective Decision-Making with Markov Processes
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh, Students

detail.title: On the Conditions for Utilitarian Collective Decision-Making with Markov Processes
detail.abstract: This paper investigates group decision-making with evolving preferences through the framework of Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). I adapt classical social choice theory to dynamic settings. Traditional social choice theory assumes static preferences, often overlooking the influence of previous decisions. In contrast, I extend the theory to accommodate dynamic preferences, reflecting the changing opinions within a society. My main contribution is try to present an axiomatic framework for MDP reward functions that align with Utilitarian social welfare functionals, ensuring consistency with social choice principles. I , then, illustrate how these reward functions can be constructed to aggregate individual preferences into evolving collective decisions. Additionally, I explore scenarios where social choice-theoretic axioms may not yield long-term optimal outcomes, highlighting potential challenges in dynamic applications.

title: Railroads, Market Access, and Indigenous Land Dispossession
affiliations: , Wilfrid Laurier University and University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Railroads, Market Access, and Indigenous Land Dispossession
detail.abstract: The expansion of the United States across the North American continent displaced and dispossessed hundreds of Indigenous nations. Historians have long argued that this process was hastened by improved transportation links, resulting from the construction of the railway. In this paper, we explore empirically the question of whether increased market access, as facilitated by railway building, accelerated the displacement and dispossession of Indigenous peoples and nations. Using spatial data containing all Indigenous land cessions up to 1894 in what is today the United States, we find that increases in market access increased the probability of Indigenous land cessions within that decade. Reductions in transport costs and growing populations in US counties both play important roles in explaining market access's overall effect. Finally, we find evidence that market access-induced land dispossession led to greater assimilation with settler populations, shorter heights for those born after dispossession, and modestly higher long-run incomes.

title: When are Technology Improvements Inflationary?
affiliations: HEC Montreal, European Central Bank (ECB) and ESADE Business School

detail.title: When are Technology Improvements Inflationary?
detail.abstract: We study how sector-specific technology shocks affect aggregate inflation. Using an analytically tractable production-network model, we show that the response of aggregate inflation to a favorable shock increases with the price rigidity of the shocked sector. Strikingly, inflation may riserather than fall-if the shock originates in a sector with a sufficiently above-average degree of price rigidity. This condition never holds if monetary policy does not respond to the output gap, and is weaker when the shocked sector is located downstream in the supply chain. We validate these predictions in a highly disaggregated multi-sector model, calibrated to the U.S. economy. The model implies that aggregate inflation rises when the underlying technology shock originates in 18 (out of 60) sectors. Finally, using a panel of U.S. manufacturing industries, we provide empirical evidence that supports the predicted relationship between sectoral price rigidity and the aggregate inflation response to sector-specific technology shocks.

title: An Empirical Investigation of Banks-Centric View of Monetary Policy from Pakistan
affiliations: University of Engineering and Technology Taxila - Department of Basic Sciences & Humanities, International Centre of Excellence (ICE) , Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE) and Islamic Culture Center Oslo Norway

detail.title: An Empirical Investigation of Banks-Centric View of Monetary Policy from Pakistan
detail.abstract: The banks centric-view of monetary policy works through the response of credit supply to the indicators of monetary policy such as interest rates and other policy instruments. The importance of the banks' credit supply channel came to the forefront since the 2007 worldwide depression affected badly the stability of banking sector. Yet, we know less about the relative role of banks in monetary policy transmission mechanism, especially, these impacts are observed on the basis of size of banks. This paper therefore empirically examines the impact of monetary policy on banks' lending channel of monetary policy. The robust two-step system-the Generalize Method of Moments (GMM) estimator is applied on an unbalanced panel dataset over the period 2005-2016. While estimating the effects of three alternative measures of monetary policy on banks' credit supply, several bank-specific variables are included in the specification as control variables. We provide strong evidence on the existence of banks' lending cannel in baseline model and differential impact of monetary policy measures on small versus large banks in extended model. Our findings suggest that there is a vital need to take into account the size of banks while designing the instruments of an effective monetary to manage credit supply in the economy.

title: Learning from the Loudest: Do the most Active Information Providers Sway Investors' Equity Premium Expectations?
affiliations: National Association of Insurance Commissioners

detail.title: Learning from the Loudest: Do the most Active Information Providers Sway Investors' Equity Premium Expectations?
detail.abstract: This paper studies how retail investors form-and continually reshape-their beliefs about future stock returns. Far from being anchored solely in economic fundamentals or rational expectations, investor beliefs emerge here as the outcome of an interplay among competing voices in the information ecosystem. Harnessing a uniquely comprehensive dataset of surveybased return expectations, coupled with text analyses of analyst reports and financial shows aired on 42 local news channels, I find that the sheer volume and prominence of certain analyst forecasts decisively shift investors' views on the equity risk premium. When widely visible outlets broadcast optimistic signals-particularly about earnings growth-retail expectations surge in a way that is both large and enduring, persisting for months. In contrast, less trumpeted insights from "quiet" experts are roundly ignored by the investing public, even though they contain predictive power for market returns. Remarkably, this attentiondriven learning dynamic holds across almost all demographic segments, from high-net-worth investors to novices with modest portfolios. My findings present a new framework for understanding how pockets of information can powerfully amplify or dampen collective sentiment. By revealing how specific streams of market information tip the scales of investor belief, I illuminate a potent channel through which narratives, rather than strict fundamentals alone, shape price dynamics.

title: Reproducing Kernel Methods for Machine Learning, PDEs, and Statistics with Python
affiliations: Sorbonne University, MPG-Partners and MPG Partners

detail.title: Reproducing Kernel Methods for Machine Learning, PDEs, and Statistics with Python
detail.abstract:
This monograph offers a modern presentation of kernel-based algorithms, through the prism of
reproducible numerical experiments, with a focus on applications and use cases, which are
implemented using an open-source library, CodPy (an acronym that stands for the Curse Of Di-
mensionality in PYthon). This library, primarily intended to tackle industrial use cases coming
from computational physics and mathematical finance, has found widespread applications across
various areas, such as statistics, or artificial intelligence (physic informed systems, reinforcement
learning, machine learning, generative methods, etc.). It is built upon a strategy based on the theory
of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) and the theory of optimal transport. All figures
of this book can be found separately on a companion’s website 2 with commented, reproducible
python code, in order to facilitate the diffusion of RKHS approaches to students, teachers, or
practitioners.

detail.title: Amici Curiae Civil Procedure and Antitrust Professors Brief in Support of Plaintiff-Appellee, Epic Games, Inc.

title: Industrial Production Dynamic in Q2 2025
affiliations: Gaidar Institute for Economic Policy and Gaidar Institute for Economic Policy

detail.title: Industrial Production Dynamic in Q2 2025
detail.abstract: The dynamics of industrial production in the Russian Federation in Q2 2025 showed signs of a transition to stagnation, as confirmed by the near-zero growth rates of the trend component of the industrial production index. The extractive sector had near-zero growth rates after a prolonged downward trend that has been observed since the beginning of 2022. The dynamics of manufacturing industries varied significantly depending on the sector: a steady positive trend was observed in metallurgy, transport equipment manufacturing, the chemical and food industries, while a decline was recorded in such industries as pulp and paper production and the manufacture of rubber and plastic products. A downward trend was observed in wholesale and retail trade.

title: The Growth Effects of Opening a Stock Exchange
affiliations: Rice University - Jesse H. Jones Graduate School of Business, Rice University - Jesse H. Jones Graduate School of Business and

detail.title: The Growth Effects of Opening a Stock Exchange
detail.abstract: Does opening a stock exchange improve a nation's economic growth? Using a synthetic controls approach, we estimate that opening the first exchange in a country increases national fifteen-year per capita GDP growth by more than 17 percentage points. This effect strengthens over time and is driven primarily by countries with strong governance or low pre-exchange income. We evaluate the spatial distribution of this growth effect using satellite data. We estimate that opening an exchange increases fifteen-year growth in light emissions by 40 percentage points in the city where the exchange is located. The effect is geographically concentrated within 50 miles of the exchange, consistent with a causal interpretation of our results.

title: Current Trends of Airport Privatization in India: Opportunities and Challenges
affiliations: Soka University

detail.title: Current Trends of Airport Privatization in India: Opportunities and Challenges

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not require ethical approval as it did not involve human participants, animal experiments, or the use of confidential or sensitive data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies.

detail.abstract: Until the 1990s, airports and air-related services operated under the Government of India. However, with the increase in air passengers, customs, and aircraft movements since the 1990s, there has been a growing need to develop and upgrade airport services. Additionally, the future growth of the Indian economy and airport users have further emphasized improving airport services. The Government of India (GoI) decided to commercialize and privatize the airports through the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model. There exist 15 airports under the PPP model in Greenfield and Brownfield investment. There are several challenges and constraints in PPP airports. Therefore, this paper delves into the background of the privatization of Indian airports, its characteristics, and the challenges of PPP airports.

title: Spantest: Mean-Variance Spanning Tests in R
affiliations: HEC Montreal - Department of Decision Sciences and

detail.title: Spantest: Mean-Variance Spanning Tests in R

declarations.funderStatement: Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (grant RGPIN-2022-03767).

detail.abstract: We introduce the R package spantest, which offers a comprehensive suite of portfolio spanning tests. It implements classical methods such as Huberman and Kandel (1987), Gibbons, Ross, and Shanken (1989), Kempf and Memmel (2006), Pesaran and Yamagata (2024), and Gungor and Luger (2016), alongside the recent residual-based subseries tests of Ardia and Sessinou (2024). The package supports both asset-level and global hypothesis testing and incorporates the Cauchy Combination Test (CCT), enabling robust inference in the presence of serial dependence, heteroskedasticity, and high-dimensional settings.

title: Conversations *
affiliations: University of Arizona - Department of Economics

detail.title: Conversations *
detail.abstract: In a conversation interlocutors talk without constraints on talking order or duration. The contents of simultaneous messages are assumed to get lost. By equating messages with disclosures of singleton subsets of interlocutors' possibility sets we endow them with literal meanings. Literal-meaning strategies minimize inferences from disclosures. All other strategies are pragmatic-meaning strategies. With common knowledge of possibility sets' sizes, optimal literal-meaning strategies let only the better-informed player talk. Optimal pragmatic-meaning strategies are strictly better and generally require that with positive probability both players talk simultaneously. With uncertain sizes of possibility sets, both players talk also in optimal literal-meaning strategies.

title: International Law as a Cyborg Science
affiliations: The University of Manchester - School of Law

detail.title: International Law as a Cyborg Science
detail.abstract: International law academics have increasingly turned to engage deliberately engage computer-oriented technologies. There is little work in the literature that reflects on how this engagement itself takes place, what it tells us about the state of the discipline, and the consequences of concentrating on the phenomena of digital technologies. This paper shares some possible conceptual taxonomies and theoretical concerns in disciplinary self-reflection about our digital futures.

title: AI Partnerships and Competition: Damned if You Buy, Damned if You Don't
affiliations: Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, International Center for Law & Economics (ICLE) and International Center for Law & Economics (ICLE)

detail.title: AI Partnerships and Competition: Damned if You Buy, Damned if You Don't
detail.abstract:
Generative "artificial intelligence" (AI) has sparked an industry-wide scramble among incumbent digital platforms to participate in the industry and/or embed artificial intelligence into their core services. Instead of full acquisitions, so-called "big tech" firms like Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, and Apple are increasingly entering strategic “AI partnerships”—notably through licensing, minority equity stakes, and infrastructure or talent sharing. Some consider that these partnerships are mainly driven by an intention to sidestep regulatory (i.e., merger control) scrutiny and, therefore, propose that they are subject to special attention from competition agencies and/or changes to current merger enforcement rules (e.g., lowering thresholds).

Our research finds that these partnerships are largely benign from a competition law perspective. Antitrust authorities across jurisdictions have, to date, identified only theoretical concerns; no enforcement body has found concrete evidence of anticompetitive harm or conduct arising from these partnerships. Moreover, these partnerships may actually enhance competition, providing startups with access to essential capital, distribution networks, and technical infrastructure—without sacrificing autonomy. In rapidly evolving AI markets, overly broad enforcement could stifle innovation and legal predictability. This paper thus argues that the default presumption should favor dynamic efficiency and contestable market growth, not expansion of merger jurisdiction, absent clear proof of competitive harm.

title: Strategic Information Transmission in the Employment Relationship *
affiliations: University of Arizona - Department of Economics and University of Arizona - Department of Economics

detail.title: Strategic Information Transmission in the Employment Relationship *
detail.abstract: Formal procedures for dealing with information in organizations may be costly to set up. Informal ones may be more vulnerable to opportunism. We study the tradeoffs by introducing strategic communication a la Crawford and Sobel (1982) into Simon's (1951) model of the employment relationship. A contract specifies the principal's "range of authority" and a fixed wage for the agent. With extreme conflict, optimal contracts minimize the range of authority and preclude communication. With little conflict they maximize the range of authority and induce influential communication. In the uniform-quadratic case, they divide the state space into approximately equalsized topics.

title: Do Extreme Weather Events Induce R&D and Other Innovation Expenditure: Evidence from Indian Manufacturing Firms
affiliations: Institute of Economic Growth (IEG) and

detail.title: Do Extreme Weather Events Induce R&D and Other Innovation Expenditure: Evidence from Indian Manufacturing Firms
detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between the innovation expenditure intensity in industrial firms and extreme weather events. Changing climate and extreme weather events adversely affect labour productivity, and firms are likely to undertake innovative actions to mitigate the deleterious effects. We measure the relationships between the expenditure on R&D activities and technology imports made by firms and temperature levels experienced by them for a panel of more than 2000 manufacturing firms in India from 2004-05 to 2015-16, spread over 350 different districts in India. We find a positive association between the extreme temperature in a year and the intensity of expenditure on R&D and technology imports of manufacturing firms, supporting the endogenous adaptation hypothesis. Moreover, we find that investments in R&D and imported technology mitigate the adverse effects of climate change on labour productivity. Our results show that the adverse effects of extreme temperature on labour productivity are larger for firms that do not invest in innovative activities.

title: Company Names, Weak Marks, and Regulatory Missteps: A Critical Analysis of the FastestCakes Case
affiliations: University of Edinburgh - School of Law, Babcock University - School of Law and Security Studies

detail.title: Company Names, Weak Marks, and Regulatory Missteps: A Critical Analysis of the FastestCakes Case
detail.abstract:
This article analyzes the conflict between a Lagos-based business’ trademark “FastestCakes” and an Ibadan-based business company name registration “Fastest Cakes in Ibadan” with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC). While the CAC ordered the Ibadan company to change its name because of an existing trademark “FastestCakes”, the paper argues that the true fault lies with the Nigerian Trademarks Office for registering “FastestCakes,” a mark that is merely descriptive and arguably generic.

 

By situating the dispute within the spectrum of trademark distinctiveness, the article shows that “FastestCakes” lacks inherent registrability and would face similar barriers internationally absent acquired distinctiveness. It further distinguishes “company names” under the Companies and Allied Matters Act, 2020 (CAMA) from “trademarks”, noting that descriptiveness is not a bar to company registration.

 

The paper contrasts this case with Sanofi S.A. v. Sanofi Integrated Services Ltd (2023), where a fanciful, distinctive mark was properly enforced against infringing company names. In FastestCakes, however, the article argues that the CAC’s reliance on a flawed (Nigerian Trademarks Office) registration addresses the consequence rather than the cause of the problem at hand. As such, the CAC ought to direct its concerns to the Nigerian Trademarks Office (the cause of the problem), and not to the owners of Fastest Cakes in Ibadan over a similar company name and an existing “trademark” (the consequence). The article concludes that stricter scrutiny of descriptive marks is necessary to preserve the integrity of Nigeria’s trademark system to avoid needless conflicts as in the FastestCakes case.

title: What can LLMs tell us about the ETI?
affiliations: University of South Carolina - Moore School of Business - Department of Economics and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: What can LLMs tell us about the ETI?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the capacity of large language models (LLMs) to approximate the elasticity of taxable income (ETI), a central parameter in public finance. Using simulations of controlled experiments and replications of studies using observational data, we evaluate how LLMs respond to tax schedule changes. Our results show that LLMs reproduce key behavioral patterns observed in human studies, though often with heightened responsiveness, suggesting limited recognition of real-world frictions. Findings suggest LLMs' potential as low-cost, flexible complements to traditional methods for analyzing taxpayer behavior and policy design, although further validation across models and contexts is needed.

title: Trust in Politicians and Preferences Over False Positive and Negative Errors in News Reports
affiliations: Hitotsubashi University - Graduate School of Economics and Academia Sinica - Institute of Political Science

detail.title: Trust in Politicians and Preferences Over False Positive and Negative Errors in News Reports
detail.abstract: This study investigates how trust in politicians shapes citizens' news consumption preferences. We focus on two dimensions of media accuracy-false-positive and false-negative errors in the reporting on political scandals-and hypothesize that political trust alters citizens' preferences for avoiding these two errors in a different way. To test this, we conducted a survey experiment combining information provision treatment with a conjoint design in Japan. We found that citizens value both types of accuracy, and that increased political trust reduces the preference for avoiding false-negative errors, but has no significant effect on the preference for avoiding false-positive errors. The treatment reduces even the preference for avoiding false-positive errors among the supporters of governing parties. Our findings suggest that political trust affects the type of media citizens prefer, which has important implications for electoral accountability.

title: The Media Coverage of Female Scholars: Evidence for the Finance, Economics, And Business Disciplines
affiliations: Luiss Guido Carli University - Department of Business and Management, Queen Mary University of London and University of London - Birkbeck College

detail.title: The Media Coverage of Female Scholars: Evidence for the Finance, Economics, And Business Disciplines

declarations.funderStatement: The authors acknowledge generous support by AFFECT (Academic Female Finance Committee) and the Journal of Financial Economics that made this research project possible.

detail.abstract: We provide systematic evidence on the media coverage of finance, economics and business scholars from research-intensive universities in the United States. First, only 40% of media appearances are about specific research, highlighting the role of academics as experts in the public realm. Second, male scholars are 42% more likely to appear in any media articles, and, among those that receive any coverage, appear in 14% more articles. This gap is most pronounced for financial economists and it can only be partially explained by scarcity of senior women and differences in research productivity. We provide evidence consistent with demand-side explanations: male journalists are less likely to cite female researchers; and female authors are less likely to be named in articles about papers with mixed-gender author teams. In contrast, female researchers are just as likely to be quoted, suggesting that they do not engage in less outreach. We provide a public version of our data on media coverage.

title: Endogenous Energy Efficiency and Residential Energy Consumption in the Presence of Health and Education Choices
affiliations: Université d'Angers (France), GRANEM - TEPP

detail.title: Endogenous Energy Efficiency and Residential Energy Consumption in the Presence of Health and Education Choices
detail.abstract: We build an overlapping-generation model with heterogenous agents, in which education, health and energy efficiency choices are endogenous. It incorporates the empirical evidence that education is positively influenced by health, and that low energy efficiency reduces health status. Firstly, this model replicates the well-documented positive relationship between energy efficiency and income level. Secondly, it shows that a greater level of energy efficiency chosen by individuals reduces wage inequality between skilled and unskilled workers. Thirdly, it replicates the positive link between the aggregate energy efficiency index (defined as the weighted sum of the individual energy efficiencies chosen) and aggregate energy consumption, as highlighted in the literature, offering a possible explanation of the rebound effect based on health and educational dimensions.

title: Equality Before Tax Law
affiliations: Michigan State University College of Law

detail.title: Equality Before Tax Law
detail.abstract:
The income tax code is riddled with exceptions—exclusions, rate preferences, and deductions—that reduce tax burdens for dominant majorities and powerful interest groups. These carveouts now amount to an astonishing $1.9 trillion, equivalent to seventy-five percent of all federal income tax revenue. By granting policymakers discretion to allocate tax exceptions, the tax system not only invites capture but also the weaponization of taxation against disfavored economic and political groups. Yet despite the central role of these exceptions, tax scholars have not articulated a principle requiring taxation according to general rules. 

This Article draws on philosophy of law to reveal an overarching tax principle that grounds the ideal tax system and supports the elimination of most exceptions. Equality before the law requires that laws are general and apply to the broadest possible category of individuals. This Article examines how this principle reshapes the three fundamental choices in tax design: the choice of the tax base, the structure of the rate schedule, and the adoption of special provisions, such as deductions. First, the tax base should be broad and encompass general economic events or situations that anyone may encounter, e.g., income or consumption. Second, the rate structure should be uniform, applying the same tax schedule to every tax base. Third, there should be no deductions that reduce final tax liabilities between taxpayers. 

This Article is the first to reveal the philosophical foundations of a broad base and a uniform rate in tax law. Upholding equality before tax law advances the twin aims of tax law—raising revenue and doing so equitably—while also providing safeguards against the threats of capture and political weaponization. This Article further shows that equality before the law mandates replacing targeted social welfare measures in tax law into universal welfare programs on the spending side. This will boost the overall redistributive force of the tax-and-transfer system as a whole.

title: Forecasting Probability Distributions of Financial Returns with Deep Neural Networks
affiliations: TripleSun

detail.title: Forecasting Probability Distributions of Financial Returns with Deep Neural Networks
detail.abstract: This study evaluates deep neural networks for forecasting probability distributions of financial returns. 1D convolutional neural networks (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architectures are used to forecast parameters of three probability distributions: Normal, Student's t, and skewed Student's t. Using custom negative log-likelihood loss functions, distribution parameters are optimized directly. The models are tested on six major equity indices (S&P 500, BOVESPA, DAX, WIG, Nikkei 225, and KOSPI) using probabilistic evaluation metrics including Log Predictive Score (LPS), Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS), and Probability Integral Transform (PIT). Results show that deep learning models provide accurate distributional forecasts and perform competitively with classical GARCH models for Value-at-Risk estimation. The LSTM with skewed Student's t distribution performs best across multiple evaluation criteria, capturing both heavy tails and asymmetry in financial returns. This work shows that deep neural networks are viable alternatives to traditional econometric models for financial risk assessment and portfolio management.

title: The Evolution of Acquihires 2.0
affiliations: Arkstons Investments Limited, Arkstons Advisory WLL,  London Business School, Department of Finance, St Anne's College, the University of Oxford, Oakcapita Advisory LLP and Independent

detail.title: The Evolution of Acquihires 2.0
detail.abstract: Acquihires have moved from distressed exits to a deliberate way to secure cohesive, IP-rich teams in AI, cybersecurity, and robotics. This paper defines “Acquihires 2.0,” explains the shift, and pinpoints the drivers: structural talent scarcity, a tougher funding cycle, and tighter merger scrutiny. We map the current deal toolkit reverse acquihires, licensing-plus-talent structures, and performance-tied equity and show why outcomes hinge on retention, cultural fit, and integration planning rather than headline price. Examples illustrate how acquirers transfer capabilities while keeping regulatory risk in bounds, often via licensing arrangements paired with selective team hiring. We also outline investor return models and practical term-sheet provisions that help VCs recover capital in flat or down rounds without burning relationship equity. The result is a clear framework for when to use acquihires, how to value them, and how to structure governance, IP, and retention so acquirers build durable capacity, founders preserve reputation, and investors see credible liquidity pathways.

reference: Columbia Business School Research Paper No. 5438154
title: Performance, Risk, and Persistence in Multi-Manager vs. Single-Manager Hedge Funds
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School

detail.title: Performance, Risk, and Persistence in Multi-Manager vs. Single-Manager Hedge Funds

publicationDetails.detailsText: Columbia Business School Research Paper No. 5438154
publicationDetails.journalName: Columbia Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive comparison between multi-manager hedge funds and traditional single-manager hedge funds, across performance, risk management, compensation structures, and operational efficiency. Multi-manager funds, known as "pods," allocate capital across multiple portfolio managers to diversify risk, while single managers rely on a single manager or team for focused strategies. Using a dataset of 50 multi-managers and 50 single-managers from 2010 to 2025, sourced from the Hedge Fund Research (HFR) database, we analyze annualized returns, Sharpe ratios, volatility, and operational metrics. Findings indicate that pods achieve lower volatility (average standard deviation of 8.2% vs. 12.5% for single-managers) but generate lower alpha (1.2% vs. 2.8%). Pods face higher turnover (15% annual PM turnover vs. 5% for single-managers) and charge higher fees (2.5% management fee vs. 1.8%). Single-managers exhibit higher risk but offer potential for outsized returns in favorable markets. Compensation at pods favors top performers, with portfolio managers earning millions or even tens of millions in years of strong performance, while single-managers provide relative stability. These findings inform investors about trade-offs in hedge fund structures and highlight the "pod model" as superior between the two.

reference: MacIsaac, S. And Wavrock, D. (2025). Renters' shelter costs by duration of tenancy. Economic and Social Reports, 5(8), 1-14. https://doi.org/10.25318/36280001202500800003-eng
title: Renters' Shelter Costs by Duration of Tenancy
affiliations: Statistics Canada and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Renters' Shelter Costs by Duration of Tenancy

publicationDetails.detailsText: MacIsaac, S. And Wavrock, D. (2025). Renters' shelter costs by duration of tenancy. Economic and Social Reports, 5(8), 1-14. https://doi.org/10.25318/36280001202500800003-eng

detail.abstract: Renters’ shelter costs can vary substantially by duration of tenancy. Renters who recently moved into their dwelling can pay substantially more than longstanding renters. This tenure-based discrepancy in rents paid can have important implications in terms of discouraging residential mobility and, by extension, Canadian labour mobility. Evicted tenants could face steep housing cost increases. In more dire cases, these increases can lead to rises in homelessness or individuals resorting to other inadequate housing alternatives. Moreover, there is a risk of discouraging residential mobility and, by extension, Canadian labour mobility. Using data from the Census of Population and the National Household Survey, this study sheds light on trends in shelter cost differences by duration of tenancy from 1996 to 2021, and how this gap in rental costs between recent renters and longer-term renters varies across municipalities and neighbourhoods. Findings show that the gap between recent and long-term renters’ shelter costs has widened over the study period and that tenure-based gaps in rental costs are pervasive beyond the priciest housing markets of Toronto and Vancouver. Accounting for comparable dwellings and neighbourhoods, longstanding tenants of five or more years paid approximately 19% less in monthly shelter costs than recent renters (under one year) in 2021 compared with 6% in 1996. The percentage of renters residing in the same dwelling they did five years ago increased from 30% to 42% of all renters during that period.

title: Ladies First? The Tax Code Says Otherwise
affiliations: University of Akron - The George W. Daverio School of Accountancy and College of Management

detail.title: Ladies First? The Tax Code Says Otherwise
detail.abstract:
Tax policy is not just about revenue.  It shapes economic opportunity, workforce participation, and financial security.  Yet, the U.S. tax code remains built on outdated assumptions about work and family, reinforcing economic dependence instead of promoting financial autonomy.  It penalizes secondary earners, ignores unpaid labor, and continues to disadvantage secondary provider (mainly women, for non-tax reasons) in ways that limit their economic choices and long-term financial stability, and which perpetuate the exclusion of approximately half the population from the labor market while severely damaging the country's GDP and aggregate economic welfare.

This Article exposes how tax laws, which are often viewed as impartial or fair, have long served to entrench inequality.  The structure of joint filing, benefit phaseouts, and tax credits such as the Earned Income Tax Credit create hidden disincentives that discourage full workforce participation and wealth accumulation.  These policies do not just harm individuals.  They weaken labor market efficiency, restrict productivity, and suppress economic growth.  A tax system that sidelines half the population is not just unfair, it is an economic miscalculation with consequences for everyone.

Ignoring these realities comes at a cost.  Achieving tax equity is not about special interests, it is about unlocking the full potential of the economy.  When tax policy discourages participation and limits financial independence, it holds back innovation, shrinks GDP, and restricts long-term prosperity.  A better approach would remove penalties on work, recognize the economic contributions of caregiving, and modernize tax structures to reflect contemporary realities.  This Article makes the case that tax reform is not just a policy debate.  It is a national economic imperative that affects us all.

title: Understanding Cross-Cultural Variability in Social Trust: Tests of the Role of Parasite Stress and Bioclimatic Endowments
affiliations: Radboud University

detail.title: Understanding Cross-Cultural Variability in Social Trust: Tests of the Role of Parasite Stress and Bioclimatic Endowments
detail.abstract: As a lubricant for interpersonal exchange, social trust is essential for the functioning of societies. One of the most striking manifestations of cross-cultural psychological diversity, then, is the huge variability in social trust across societies, specifically geopolitical units. However, we lack understanding of the origins of social trust as one and perhaps the most important feature of human cultures. This study considered two theoretical perspectives of ecological factors explaining why some societies are so much more trusting than other societies are. The first perspective proposes parasite stress and associated behavioral immune defenses as predictors of social trust. The second perspective proposes bioclimatic endowments such as the availability of domesticable plants and animals and associated subsistence systems as historical drivers of trust. Empirical tests indicated that the prevalence of non-zoonotic parasites is a more powerful predictor of social trust than are ecological factors related to subsistence systems. However, the impact of absolute latitude rendered all these factors insignificant. A puzzle remains, as we uncovered no evidence as to the mechanism underlying the latitudinal gradient in social trust. Advancing on this puzzle, as well as on understanding psychological diversity between human populations more generally, requires development of novel theories and empirical approaches.

title: (When) Can Trade Wars Be Good?
affiliations: Singapore Management University - Yong Pung How School of Law and University of New South Wales (UNSW) - UNSW Law & Justice

detail.title: (When) Can Trade Wars Be Good?
detail.abstract: “Trade wars are good, and easy to win,” tweeted Donald Trump in 2018. The US–China trade war that followed proved otherwise - especially when confronting a major economic power. Yet, can trade wars ever be good? While the academic consensus holds they harm all participants, we argue that under certain circumstances they can produce positive outcomes. Set against the backdrop of the Liberation Day tariffs announced on April 2, 2025, this paper examines the limits of the Ricardian free trade model underpinning the current multilateral trading system, identifies when trade wars may serve strategic goals, and explores alternative rules to address state-capitalist distortions without costly, prolonged conflict.

title: Debt Maturity and Innovation: A Reconsideration
affiliations: , University of Sussex Business School and

detail.title: Debt Maturity and Innovation: A Reconsideration
detail.abstract: We study an incomplete contracting setting in which an entrepreneur seeks funding for a project and can privately choose its type. Renegotiation is permitted at an intermediate date. We identify the conditions under which short-term or callable long-term debt can incentivize the entrepreneur to undertake the value-maximizing project. We show that even when pay-for-failure is necessary, callable long-term debt contract can replicate the state-contingent contract for a strictly positive measure of parameters.

title: Endogenous Kinship Institutions.
affiliations: , University of Bologna and Department of Economics, University of Bologna

detail.title: Endogenous Kinship Institutions.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have no relevant material interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: No human participant involved.
declarations.funderStatement: 2015 Rita Levi-Montalcini program and the 2022 PRIN program (Prot. 2022SA485H 001; CUP J53D23004930006)

detail.abstract: Kinship structures the patterns of human relationships within the family, whereby matrilineal succession is believed to weaken both the males' authority and their incentives to cooperate. To evaluate this conjecture, we study a society equally split in males and females interested in maximizing the return on their joint investment by selecting property rights shaping their ex post bargaining power. The investment return is determined by both a couple-specific technological parameter and the product of the parties' non-contractible time allocations in farming and home production. Being-on average-farming the most productive activity, society achieves the first best by fully protecting either side when they are better at farming and by favoring the party with the lowest farming productivity otherwise. While in the first case couples specialize in farming, in the second one, more productive couples focus on farming and less productive ones diversify. Ultimately, society embraces matrilineal succession when females are less productive than males and patriliny otherwise. Crucially, this prediction is consistent, across identification strategies, with a novel regional data set of the kinship institutions and farming productivity observed over the 600-1550 CE period in the Ghana, Mali and Songhai empires. Notably, temperature drops, which increased the yield of plow-positive crops and in turn, the male farming productivity, induced reforms towards matrilineal succession. Crucially, the latter are negatively related to the proxy for matrilineal inheritance of real property devised by the Ethnographic Atlas.

title: The Effects of Exchange Rate Movements on Publicly Traded US Corporations
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School

detail.title: The Effects of Exchange Rate Movements on Publicly Traded US Corporations

keywords: and Financial Market Reactions JEL codes: F14

detail.abstract: Previous literature struggled to find strong effects of exchange-rate exposure on US stock returns. Our paper brings firm-specific export data to reinvestigate this exchangerate puzzle, and finds surprisingly large exchange-rate effects on exports, sales, profits, and stock returns. These were not offset by (financial or operational) hedging, and they seem to have not only been due to export changes but also due to changes in the domestic competitive environment. The effects increased over time and were stronger for larger and more export-oriented firms.

title: Economic Diversification Potential: Insights from Mongolia's Livestock Product Value Chains

declarations.funderStatement: The authors declare that no funds, grants, or other support were received during the preparation of this manuscript.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Studies in Agricultural Economics, 0[10.7896/j.3036]

detail.abstract: Mongolia, endowed with abundant natural resources, faces a critical challenge in reducing its reliance on the mining sector and achieving economic diversification. This study aims to identify economic diversification potential for developing the non-mining processing industry. To this end, a Revealed Comparative Advantage (RCA) analysis and value chain mapping were employed. The RCA results highlight the importance of livestock-derived products and recognise the livestock sector as having the best potential for achieving economic diversification. Consequently, the value chain of livestock-derived products was mapped and key challenges at each stage were identified. The study provides actionable recommendations for developing the value chain of livestock-derived products. The findings underscore that the value chain of livestock-derived products encounters numerous obstacles that must abe addressed to build a competitive sector. Key strategies include improving animal health, ensuring compliance with good practices and standards, and enhancing competitiveness through advanced technologies, increased financial and investment support, and improved logistics and infrastructure. These measures are essential for achieving Mongolia's economic diversification objectives.

reference: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-119
title: Chat2Learn: A Proof-of-Concept Evaluation of a Technology-Based Tool to Enhance Parent-Child Language Interaction
affiliations: University of Chicago and University of Chicago

detail.title: Chat2Learn: A Proof-of-Concept Evaluation of a Technology-Based Tool to Enhance Parent-Child Language Interaction

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-119
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Parental language input is essential for children’s early language development, yet substantial disparities persist in both its quantity and quality. Most early language interventions adopt an explicit theory of change, educating parents about why and how to talk with their children, but such approaches tend to be resource-intensive, which limit their potential for scalability. The present study examines Chat2Learn, a low-cost, text-messaging tool that delivers open-ended prompts designed to elicit decontextualized conversations among parent-child dyads. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory, Chat2Learn aims to reduce parents’ extraneous load of generating conversational topics, thereby increasing opportunities for rich parent–child interactions. Participants were 63 parent–child dyads (children ages 3–6; 65.1% girls) recruited from preschool programs serving families in under-resourced neighborhoods in Chicago. They were randomly assigned to an experimental condition, where parents had access to Chat2Learn, or a business-as-usual control condition, during a 10-minute unstructured waiting period. Results showed that parents in the Chat2Learn condition spent less time inattentive or withdrawn during interactions (p = .05).  Chat2Learn parents also produced higher-quality language input, including longer utterances, more unique words, and more open-ended questions, compared to controls (all p’s < .05). No immediate differences emerged in children’s language output. These findings provide a proof-of-concept that an intervention that takes a learning by doing approach in providing concrete support for parents with 'what to talk about' rather than abstract training in 'why" and "how' to talk can positively shift parent–child interaction patterns.

title: Classifying US Firms into Trade Peace and Trade War Stocks: an NLP Analysis of Earnings Call Transcripts Approach (slides)

detail.title: Classifying US Firms into Trade Peace and Trade War Stocks: an NLP Analysis of Earnings Call Transcripts Approach (slides)
detail.abstract:
Objective: Assess firms’ sensitivity to global trade shocks by classifying them as trade peace or trade war stocks.
Approach: Apply NLP techniques to 54,851 earnings call transcripts (Russell 1000, 2007–2025)
Evaluation: Event study on cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) around major trade policy events

title: Classifying US Firms into Trade Peace and Trade War Stocks: an NLP Analysis of Earnings Call Transcripts Approach
affiliations: Paris Dauphine University, Students and Paris Dauphine University, Students

detail.title: Classifying US Firms into Trade Peace and Trade War Stocks: an NLP Analysis of Earnings Call Transcripts Approach
detail.abstract: Global trade developments can affect firms’ performance, particularly for companies with significant international exposure. Understanding how sensitive individual firms are to trade-related shocks and classifying them as “trade peace” (benefiting from trade policy shocks) or “trade war” stocks is crucial for investors, policymakers, and corporate decision-makers. This study proposes an approach to classify firms’ trade sensitivity by applying Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to 54,851 earnings call transcripts of Russell 1000 constituents from 2007 to 2025. We employ bag-of-words (BoW), sentimentadjusted BoW (BoWws), TF-IDF combined with logistic regression, and FinBERT, a transformer-based financial language model, to extract textual signals related to trade exposure. Firms are classified as trade peace or trade war stocks based on model predictions, and we evaluate the economic relevance of these classifications through an event study of cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) around major trade policy events. Our findings suggest that while none of the models clearly discriminate between trade peace and trade war stocks in terms of opposite-signed CAR differences, the TF-IDF–logistic regression model achieves the largest absolute difference in mean cross-sectional CARs, equal to 1.29%. These results highlight the potential of earnings call transcripts as a source for measuring firms’ trade sensitivity and provide insights into the strengths and limitations of various NLP-based approaches for classifying firms’ exposure to global trade shocks.

reference: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-121
title: Laboratories of Autocracy: Landscape of Central-Local Dynamics in China's Policy Universe
affiliations: , University of Chicago and Harvard University

detail.title: Laboratories of Autocracy: Landscape of Central-Local Dynamics in China's Policy Universe

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-121
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Using a comprehensive collection of 3.7 million Chinese policy documents and government work reports spanning the past two decades, we identify 115,679 distinct policies and systematically trace their initiation and diffusion. Our analysis reveals three key findings. First, China's policymaking has historically been highly decentralized, with local bureaucrats playing crucial roles in both creating new policies and spreading them. Second, since 2013, policymaking has become substantially more centralized, driven primarily by changing bureaucratic incentivesbottom-up innovation is no longer rewarded, while strict enforcement of central policies is. Third, our examination of industrial policies shows that centralization affects both policy suitability and effectiveness. Top-down industrial policies tend to align poorly with local conditions and are less effective at driving industrial growth, highlighting centralization's costs. On the other hand, under decentralization, competition among local officials can distort policy diffusion, also undermining effectiveness. Our quantitative assessment of both distortions indicates that economic costs of centralizing policymaking in China have significantly outweighed its benefits.

title: Revaluation Alpha
affiliations: Research Affiliates, LLC, Northern Illinois University - Department of Finance, Duke University - Fuqua School of Business and Research Affiliates, LLC

detail.title: Revaluation Alpha
detail.abstract: We define revaluation return as the portion of a factor's historical return that comes from changes in its valuation ratio. A factor may have impressive historical performance, but if the high return was driven by rising valuations, it is unwise to expect similar future returns because valuation ratios cannot rise indefinitely, and often mean-revert. We define structural return as the historical factor return net of the revaluation return. For decades, the factor literature has implicitly assumed that revaluation alpha is equally predictive to structural alpha. We challenge that assumption. Structural returns predict future returns better than raw historical returns and add incremental value beyond well-known timing signals such as momentum.

reference: New York University Stern School of Business Research Paper Series
title: Green Moral Hazard: Estimating the Financial and Non-financial Impacts of CEO Incentives

detail.title: Green Moral Hazard: Estimating the Financial and Non-financial Impacts of CEO Incentives

publicationDetails.detailsText: New York University Stern School of Business Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: I develop a novel structural model and analyze the financial and non-financial implications of CEO compensation contracts that include incentives tied to non-financial performance. By applying this model to green incentives, I find that they motivate CEOs to reduce carbon emission intensity by 1.8% per year but at a financial cost of 1.3% of firm value annually. As green performance is an imperfect signal of CEOs' actions toward green outcomes, a "green moral hazard" arises: the principal should offer CEOs a premium for the risk added by green incentives. I estimate that this green moral hazard is substantial, accounting for $1.72 million of the total moral hazard cost of $2.05 million. These results suggest that green incentives pose an important economic trade-off: while green incentives can lead to meaningful environmental improvements, they impose substantial costs on the firm.

title: Why Financial Economics Cannot Explain Financial Management
affiliations: ISEG, Universidade de Lisboa

detail.title: Why Financial Economics Cannot Explain Financial Management
detail.abstract: Financial economics generally claims that financial management is either irrelevant or relevant merely because of supposed market imperfections. This study presents an alternative explanation: 'in our monetary societies financial management is a significant activity for organizations, societies, and the human-relationship with the biosphere'. Accordingly, it discusses two hypotheses with excess content in relation to the Fisher-Modigliani-Miller capital-income theory, which is the cornerstone of capital-structure management theories in financial economics (e.g., trade-off theory, pecking-order theory, and market-timing theory). The first mechanical-effect hypothesis suggests that the empirical relationship between the market-to-book value of a firm (or Tobin-q) and its capital structure is not due to the market's ability to identify intangible assets and growth opportunities, but rather because of the market-to-book variable's computational procedure. We add a new hypothesis, namely, that for computational reasons, the empirical behavior of the market-to-book of the firm and market-tobook of equity is only similar when both variables are close to or equal to 1. We tested conventional and big data methods on large samples of firms from eight-countries. The findings demonstrate the unsustainability of financial economics in explaining real-life organizations, societies, and environmental phenomena. Hence, we contribute theoretical and empirical support for research on alternative explanations.

title: Anomalies and Cash Flows
affiliations: University of Arizona - Eller College of Management

detail.title: Anomalies and Cash Flows
detail.abstract: I examine whether stock market anomalies reflect risk compensation or mispricing by analyzing their underlying cash-flow patterns. I distinguish between discrete anomalies based on information events (e.g., profitability) and continuous anomalies lacking such coordinating events (e.g., idiosyncratic volatility). Discrete anomalies exhibit procyclical cash-flow patterns consistent with risk-based pricing. In contrast, continuous anomalies show countercyclical cash-flow patterns that hedge macroeconomic conditions. Building upon Hong and Stein's (1999) gradual information diffusion framework, I develop a model illustrating the effects of discrete and continuous information arrival on price dynamics. The model shows that discrete information causes immediate price adjustment due to coordinated trading prompted by the simultaneous revelation of information; continuous information leads to initial investor underreaction, subsequent overreaction, and eventual correction. I highlight the important role of the information environment in reflecting the fundamental sources of anomaly returns.

reference: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series No. 234
title: Kalecki and the Stucturalist View of Economic Development
affiliations: University of London - School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS)

detail.title: Kalecki and the Stucturalist View of Economic Development

publicationDetails.detailsText: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series No. 234
publicationDetails.journalName: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper commemorates the 70 th anniversary of Kalecki's seminal lecture in Mexico on financing economic development. The first part of this paper outlines the theoretical model underlying Kalecki's view of development financing. A second part of the paper summarizes the foundations of structuralist development economics in the Prebisch-Singer approach to international trade and import-substitution development strategies. A third part of the paper examines the confrontation between Kalecki's view of economic development strategy, and the structuralist approach, in the case of Cuba, highlighting the differences between the two approaches. A fourth part concludes with some reflections on the relevance today of structuralism and Kalecki’s view of economic development.

title: On the Rocks: The WTO’s Member-Driven, Consensus Decision-Making
affiliations: Queen's University - School of Policy Studies and WTO Secretariat

detail.title: On the Rocks: The WTO’s Member-Driven, Consensus Decision-Making
detail.abstract: The buzzword for the troubled World Trade Organization (WTO) is 'reform'. But without a shared view of what that means, reform cannot begin in any meaningful way. There is no doubt that two of the WTO's functions are floundering: negotiating new rules and settling legal disputes about compliance with existing rules-but even then, member governments have found ways of producing some results. A third function is working better: the scrutiny of trade measures in the regular committees on the various WTO agreements. It sustains a considerable amount of rules-compliant trade, although that too should be improved. The failing is collective even if some countries or groups of countries might take more of the blame than others.

title: Flight to Safety or Flight from Carry?
affiliations: State Street Associates, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Harvard Business School - Finance Unit

detail.title: Flight to Safety or Flight from Carry?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Cheema-Fox and Cuipa are employed by State Street Bank; Greenwood is an affiliate of State Street and at Harvard Business School.
declarations.funderStatement: State Street Bank

detail.abstract: This paper examines the distinction between safe-haven and funding currencies during periods of market stress, focusing on how global institutional investors allocate across currencies during crisis episodes. Using FX forward and sovereign bond flows from a major custodian bank, the study finds that while the CHF, JPY, and USD often attract inflows during crises, their roles can diverge. For example, the USD saw inflows during the Global Financial Crisis and major geopolitical shocks, while the 2024 carry crash centered on the JPY. A panel regression framework using institutional investor flows is developed to classify crises as either flights to safety or flights from carry. Carry was a larger factor than safe-haven demand in driving flows around Liberation Day. The distinction between carry and safety driven flows has become more important in recent years as USD rates have risen while those on CHF and JPY instruments have remained low.
