As a result, the securitization of stablecoins under the Investment Securities Act(ISA)of 2025 is misguided and counterproductive, diverging from function-based regulatory models exemplified by the EU's MiCA Regulation and the US's CLARITY Act.

title: Disaggregated Geopolitical Risks and Global Stock Returns
affiliations: University of Turku - Turku School of Economics and Department of Accounting and Finance, University of Turku

detail.title: Disaggregated Geopolitical Risks and Global Stock Returns
detail.abstract: We introduce a novel framework to measure how geopolitical risk exposure (GRE) affects stock returns. Using data from 40 countries over 1995-2022, we construct three factors: geopolitical risk factor (GPRF), geopolitical act factor (GPAF), and geopolitical threat factor (GPTF). This study documents four main findings. First, geopolitical threats (GPTs) have markedly stronger GRE than geopolitical acts (GPAs), with 58% of countries showing significant GPTF results vs. 35% for GPAF. Second, predictability is strongest at shorter horizons, with 68% of countries demonstrating significant one-month predictability for GPTF effects. Third, these effects persist even after accounting for established market risk factors, with 33% of countries maintaining significant GPTF relationships. Fourth, our factors provide economically meaningful out-of-sample forecasting ability, yielding positive 𝑅2 values in 60% of countries and utility gains for mean-variance investors. The findings offer a practical framework for integrating GRE assessments into portfolio management decisions.

title: Financial Intermediaries and the Yield Curve
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Financial Intermediaries and the Yield Curve

contentType.other: accepted paper, working details to be forthcoming

detail.abstract: I study the yield curve dynamics in a general equilibrium model with financial intermediaries facing financing constraints. When constraints bind, intermediaries reallocate their portfolio, causing deadweight losses in aggregate consumption, thus affecting savers' marginal utility. Because the yield curve is a forecast of marginal utility, intermediaries constraints show up, via general equilibrium forces, in longterm yields. I show that the mechanism connecting intermediaries constraints and long-term yields produces highly nonlinear interest rate dynamics and a positive real term premium in equilibrium. I extend the analysis to the nominal yield curve using a simple Taylor rule.

title: The Importance of Being Earnest (In Search Markets)
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University and University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Finance Area

detail.title: The Importance of Being Earnest (In Search Markets)
detail.abstract: In some markets for highly illiquid assets most transactions are mediated through auctions. In others it is through brokers who hold no inventory. Why? We explore this with a novel framework of decentralized markets for large indivisible assets where the central friction is buyers' difficulty to credibly convey their private valuation. We show this friction can be costly to sellers and identify a novel role for brokers as certifiers of their own clients' earnest intentions. When sellers can choose between an auction and broker-mediation, the latter dominates whenever markets are not tight and/or when buyers' private valuations are sufficiently diverse.

reference: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-120
title: Firms have Partial Knowledge: Evidence From a Reform
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Firms have Partial Knowledge: Evidence From a Reform

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-120
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: How can firms persistently misoptimize, and how can they learn? A pricing reform forced firms to adjust most prices. Because consumers exhibit left-digit bias, optimal pricing implies setting prices just below round numbers and avoiding round prices. The initial response revealed that firms operated with partial knowledge, even in the long run. Partial knowledge enables mistakes to persist. At the same time, firms were able to learn, which highlights exploration as a way to improve and lack of exploration as fostering partial knowledge. This paper encourages researchers to treat firms' misoptimization as a descriptive benchmark and urges practitioners to invest in learning processes.

title: Unfair Chances and Labor Supply
affiliations: Aarhus University, Department of Economics and Business Economics, Maastricht University and Maastricht University

detail.title: Unfair Chances and Labor Supply
detail.abstract: We conduct an online experiment to study how the unfairness of chances leading to wage inequality affects labor supply decisions. We find that, at a given wage, disadvantageous wage inequality reduces labor supply, but whether this inequality stems from fair or unfair chances does not matter. That is, a procedure with fair chances does not compensate for wage inequality. Our results stand in stark contrast to prior empirical evidence showing that individuals care about fair chances when making equity judgments.

title: Regarding the Proclamation, “Private Property is the Source of Freedom in America!”
affiliations: Seton Hall University

detail.title: Regarding the Proclamation, “Private Property is the Source of Freedom in America!”
detail.abstract: In capitalism, immorality, iniquity, vileness, or wickedness has tainted the cause of private property. History seems to agree with former US Secretary of Labor Robert B. Reich, who said: There are five ways to accumulate private property in the order of a billion dollars: (i) profiting from a monopoly, (ii) insider trading, (iii) political payoffs, (iv) fraud, and (v) inheritance. Progressive intellectuals regard America as a plutocracy rather than a democracy. Plutocratic properties are not truly private properties. They are privately controlled public properties. In a democracy, they should be either reduced to genuinely private properties through due process or publicly controlled.

title: Embarking on a New Era: Transforming Standalone B.Ed. Colleges into Multidisciplinary Institutions in Alignment with NEP 2020
affiliations: Autonomous College

detail.title: Embarking on a New Era: Transforming Standalone B.Ed. Colleges into Multidisciplinary Institutions in Alignment with NEP 2020
detail.abstract: The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 marks a transformative moment in India's higher education landscape, emphasizing flexibility, interdisciplinarity, and holistic learning. One of its most significant directives is the conversion of standalone Bachelor of Education (B.Ed.) colleges into multidisciplinary institutions by 2030. This mandate, further supported by the revised regulations of the National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE), aims to enhance the quality and relevance of teacher education by embedding it within a broader academic and research framework. This paper presents a comprehensive and phased action plan to guide B.Ed. colleges through this transition. The proposed five-phase framework encompasses: (1) Foundational Groundwork and Strategic Planning, which involves institutional auditing, stakeholder engagement, and vision-setting; (2) Academic and Infrastructural Overhaul, focusing on the introduction of the Integrated Teacher Education Programme (ITEP), curriculum redesign, and modernized infrastructure; (3) Regulatory Compliance and Affiliation, addressing accreditation, UGC/NCTE recognition, and affiliation strategies; (4) Launch and Operationalization, emphasizing admissions, marketing, and academic roll-out; and (5) Continuous Improvement and Quality Assurance, through the establishment of Internal Quality Assurance Cells (IQACs) and ongoing curriculum and institutional evaluation. The paper also highlights the importance of financial planning, policy alignment, faculty development, and community engagement to ensure the sustainability and effectiveness of the transformation. By following this structured roadmap, B.Ed. institutions can not only comply with NEP mandates but also thrive as dynamic, multidisciplinary centers for teacher education and beyond. This research contributes to policy implementation strategies and institutional reform in the Indian context.

title: Are College Exit Exams a Valid Measure of Learning? It's Complicated
affiliations: Nonpartisan Education Group

detail.title: Are College Exit Exams a Valid Measure of Learning? It's Complicated

keywords: Teaching and Learning in Higher Education

detail.abstract: Given the enormity of the public and private investment in US higher education, of course we should evaluate its effectiveness. But, how? It is claimed that over 200 higher education institutions administer the one-size-fitsall Collegiate Learning Assessment (CLA). When administered pre-post-that is, near the beginning and then again near the end of a student's program-the difference in scores on equivalent forms of the same test (i.e., the "gain score") represents how much students have learned in that program. Or does it?

reference: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, volume 2019.0, issue 48, 2019[10.17016/FEDS.2019.048]; https://www.bostonfed.org/publications/risk-and-policy-analysis/2019/reach-for-yield-by-us-public-pension-funds.aspx
title: Reach for Yield by U.S. Public Pension Funds
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Federal Reserve Bank of Boston

detail.title: Reach for Yield by U.S. Public Pension Funds

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, volume 2019.0, issue 48, 2019[10.17016/FEDS.2019.048]

detail.abstract: We theoretically model and empirically study whether U.S. public pension funds increase the riskiness of asset portfolios or net worth in response to low interest rates, underfunding, or sponsors’ fiscal condition.  We create a new methodology to infer funds’ risk from limited information on their returns and portfolio weights.  Funds took more asset risk when risk-free rates and funding ratios were lower, or when their sponsors were fiscally weaker.  In contrast, funds’ net worth risk is not explained by underfunding and weakly explained by low interest rates.  Our net worth findings suggest some funds increased asset risk to hedge liabilities.

title: Unseen Damage: Bushfire, Infant Health and Early Child Development
affiliations: Australian National University (ANU) - Crawford School of Public Policy

detail.title: Unseen Damage: Bushfire, Infant Health and Early Child Development

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest or competing interest with respect to the research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific fundings or research grants in the course of study, research or assembly of the paper. The author has no financial relationship to disclose that could be perceived as potential conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: Naturally occurring bushfires have become a global concern, with epidemiological evidence highlighting the unique toxicity of bushfire smoke compared to ambient air pollution. Leveraging remote-sensing data and a novel dynamic-radius fire assignment strategy, this paper causally examines the longitudinal impacts of in utero and neonatal bushfire smoke exposure on the medium-run health and cognitive development of Australian children, from infancy to late adolescence. The results show strong negative effects of prenatal exposure on birth outcomes, with evidence pointing to air pollution, rather than maternal stress, as the primary mechanism. Consistent with the documented resilience of female fetuses, the impact on asthma diagnosis is more pronounced among males. Neonatal exposure is associated with lower likelihood of achieving a healthy BMI before puberty and delayed development of working memory in adolescence. Further analysis highlights the nurturing aspect of parental involvement in mitigating the adverse effects of early-life exposure on later educational outcomes. A series of robustness checks were performed, with results that reinforce the main findings.

title: Remittance Inflows and Dutch Disease: The Case of Bangladesh
affiliations: Bangladesh Bank, Bangladesh Bank and Bangladesh Bank

detail.title: Remittance Inflows and Dutch Disease: The Case of Bangladesh
detail.abstract:
Using the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model and novel dynamic ARDL
(DARDL) simulations, this paper revisits the impact of remittance inflows on real exchange
rate in Bangladesh over the period 1976 to 2024. Our results show that, in
both the long and short term, remittance inflows cause a depreciation of Bangladeshi
Taka, which reject the Dutch Disease hypothesis in Bangladesh’s context. Explicitly,
we find that a 1% increase in remittance inflows causes real exchange rate to depreciate
by 0.12% and 0.11% per year in the short-run and long-run, respectively. Our DARDL
simulation results further demonstrate this relationship when we applied counterfactual
shocks on remittance inflows by 10%. We also find a long-term asymmetric impact of
remittances on real exchange rate using a non-linear ARDL (NARDL) approach. Particularly,
the positive shocks in remittance inflows depreciate the real exchange rate, while
the negative shocks cause an appreciation. In light of these empirical findings, it can
be argued that the fear of remittance inflows causing a decline in the competitiveness
of Bangladesh is not valid. However, it is important to channelize migrants’ remittance
inflows into productive investment, particularly through financial sector development
initiatives such as reinforcing financial inclusion and providing tailored financial services
to the remittance recipient families left behind.

title: The Impact of a Raw Material Import Ban on Vertical Outward FDI: Theoretical Insights and Quasi-Experimental Evidence
affiliations: University of the Sunshine Coast - Faculty of Business and James Cook University

detail.title: The Impact of a Raw Material Import Ban on Vertical Outward FDI: Theoretical Insights and Quasi-Experimental Evidence
detail.abstract: This paper examines how adverse supply-side shocks in domestic input markets influence firms' vertical outward foreign direct investment (OFDI) decisions. While the theoretical basis for cost-driven OFDI is well established, empirical evidence on the causal mechanisms remains limited. We develop a framework in which input cost shocks raise unit production costs, but firms undertake vertical OFDI only when shocks are sufficiently severe or when baseline costs are already high. Firm heterogeneity leads to a sorting pattern, whereby more productive firms are more likely to invest abroad. To test this mechanism, we exploit China's 2017 waste paper import ban as an exogenous shock and leverage a distinctive feature of the paper product industry's supply chain. Using a difference-indifferences strategy and firmlevel data from 2000 to 2023, we find that the policy shock increased the probability of vertical OFDI by approximately 16% in the post-policy period relative to a control group. These results provide robust evidence that firms respond to domestic input shocks by reallocating production across borders, highlighting vertical OFDI as a strategic response to supply-side disruptions. The findings contribute to understanding the micro-foundations of global production decisions in the face of input market volatility.

title: The Foreign Commerce Power
affiliations: Georgetown University Law Center and Duke University School of Law

detail.title: The Foreign Commerce Power
detail.abstract: This Article is the first to scrutinize presidential trade authority under the Constitution. The Constitution grants the president no independent power to regulate foreign commerce. That conclusion, while apparent from a straightforward reading of Articles I and II, stands in stark contrast to executive conduct of U.S. trade policy in recent years. This Article traces the roots of this constitutional distortion to a confluence of doctrinal drift and academic oversight. Courts and commentators have increasingly relied on an expansive conception of executive power grounded in a perceived general foreign affairs authority. In doing so, they have blurred the line between diplomacy and commerce and used this confluence to justify unilateral economic actions by a "trader-in-chief" that circumvent the allocation of power in the Constitution. These matters have reached a tipping point over the last decade, prompting a series of high-profile cases in which the government has argued that this general foreign affairs powers include some portion of the foreign commerce power. To correct this misapprehension, the Article undertakes a novel examination of Founding-era materials, including the distribution of commercial authority between the king and parliament in eighteenth century Britain, the correspondence and deliberations of the Framers, and Founding Generation's implementation of the commerce power in matters of national security during the early year of the Republic. These sources reveal a consistent and deliberate understanding both that Congress's control over foreign commerce is exclusive and that Congress's control over commerce trumps the president's general foreign affairs powers when the two intersect. The Article further argues that this allocation was not accidental or ancillary, but central to the constitutional design. As the Supreme Court prepares to confront fundamental questions concerning the scope of executive trade authority, this Article provides the necessary historical and legal framework to restore the foreign commerce power to its constitutional home.

title: Policy Gradient Methods for Optimal Trade Execution in Limit Order Books
affiliations: University of Oxford, Deutsche Bank AG (London) and University of Oxford - Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance, University of Oxford - Mathematical Institute

detail.title: Policy Gradient Methods for Optimal Trade Execution in Limit Order Books
detail.abstract: We discuss applications of policy gradient methods for the optimal execution of an asset position via limit orders. We study two examples in depth, a parametric limit order book (LOB) model and a realistic generative adversarial neural network (GAN) LOB model. In the first case, we apply a zeroth-order gradient estimator to a suitable parametrisation of candidate policies and propose modifications to lower the variance in the estimate, including conditional sampling and a backward in time recursion. In the second case, we adapt a recently published LOB GAN model to obtain a differentiable map from the parameters to the objective. We then alter a standard policy gradient method with a path-wise gradient estimator to overcome issues with the non-convexity and roughness of the loss-landscape, studying different initialization using inexact dynamic programing and second order optimisation steps, as well as regularisation of the learnt policies. In both cases, we are able to learn effective trading strategies.

title: Reducing peak load from electric vehicles through grid tariffs: Evidence from a randomized field experiment
affiliations: University of Groningen, Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM),  and Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM)

detail.title: Reducing peak load from electric vehicles through grid tariffs: Evidence from a randomized field experiment
detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) is essential for reducing CO₂ emissions, but it puts growing pressure on electricity grids by driving up peak demand. Grid tariffs can help mitigate this impact by encouraging more efficient use of grid capacity. We conduct a randomized controlled trial among more than 600 households with home EV charging to evaluate their response to a capacity-based tariff that imposes an exceedance charge on electricity consumption above a predefined capacity threshold. We test two variants: a static exceedance tariff, which charges for exceedances at all times and encourages households to reduce overall capacity use; and a Time-of-Use (TOU) exceedance tariff, which only charges for exceedances during peak hours (5 PM to 2 AM), incentivizing demand shifts to off-peak periods. We find that the static exceedance tariff reduces individual peak demand and exceedances above the threshold by approximately 5 to 10 percent, while not shifting charging to off-peak hours. In contrast, households exposed to the TOU exceedance tariff shift charging to off-peak hours after 2 AM, but without reducing individual peak demand or exceedances.  Although TOU tariffs are designed to reduce peak demand, they may unintentionally create new peaks by concentrating EV charging in the same off-peak hours, revealing a clear drawback. Our findings suggest that static exceedance tariffs may be more effective in reducing peak demand.

title: AI-Powered Scenario Planning to Foster Strategic Agility
affiliations: ESCP Business School and ESCP Business School

detail.title: AI-Powered Scenario Planning to Foster Strategic Agility

publicationDetails.journalName: ESCP Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In today's era of permacrisis, the need for innovative methods has never been more critical. Traditional approaches to strategy and decision-making cannot be scaled up and are insufficient to keep pace with the rapid changes and complexities that organizations face today. While scenario planning represents an already powerful tool, it must evolve beyond merely serving as a source of inspiration and transition into a foundation for actionable decision-making. AI plays a crucial role in this transformation, as it offers the capacity to analyze vast amounts of data and generate insights at unprecedented speed. However, AI alone is not a panacea. Human intervention remains essential, and any real progress requires a deep organizational and cultural shift. This new vision of strategy development emphasizes the synergy between AI and human expertise, moving beyond short-term tactical responses to cultivate adaptive, long-term strategic frameworks.

title: Moral Philosophy and Archetypes in the Symbolic Cohesion of the Legend of the Mohan
affiliations: EDUKIVOTOS

detail.title: Moral Philosophy and Archetypes in the Symbolic Cohesion of the Legend of the Mohan
detail.abstract: This research explores the legend of El Mohán as a cultural device intertwining moral philosophy and symbolic archetypes in Colombian tradition. Drawing on utilitarian, Kantian, and Aristotelian frameworks, the myth operates as a pedagogical tool regulating behavior, fostering virtues, and reinforcing moral duty. Its ambiguous roles—hero, antihero, villain, and anti-villain—highlight how oral tradition transmits values of social cohesion, environmental sustainability, and gender order. El Mohán demonstrates the enduring power of myth as a normative language that resists cultural homogenization and reinforces collective identity in the age of globalization.

title: Ecosystem-Level Ambidexterity and Complementors’ Category Spanning: Knowledge Search  within Vs. Outside Platform Ecosystems
affiliations: Institute of Science Tokyo

detail.title: Ecosystem-Level Ambidexterity and Complementors’ Category Spanning: Knowledge Search  within Vs. Outside Platform Ecosystems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest associated with this manuscript.
declarations.funderStatement: This study was supported by JSPS KAKENHI (Grant No. 21K13346 and 24K00287).

detail.abstract: The purpose of this study is to clarify how complementors’ category-spanning orientation in platform ecosystems relates to their degree of external knowledge search. The analysis examined the relationship between complementors’ generalist nature (i.e., category-spanning orientation) and their external knowledge search both within and outside the ecosystem. Using survey data comprising 1,078 observation samples from 98 firms in the Japanese game market, multilevel ordered logistic models with firm-level random effects were applied. Results indicate that a higher category-spanning orientation is positively associated with increased external knowledge search within the ecosystem but negatively associated with search outside the ecosystem. However, this negative association disappears and becomes positive when complementors exhibit a strong exploration orientation. These findings suggest that generalist complementors with a strong exploration orientation can facilitate both internal knowledge circulation and external knowledge inflow for the ecosystem, thereby contributing to ecosystem-level ambidexterity.

title: Taxing Powers of the European Union
affiliations: University of Passau - Law Faculty

detail.title: Taxing Powers of the European Union
detail.abstract: The European Union and its Member States are facing enormous financial challenges. To address them, the EU has not only incurred its own debt for the first time (NextGenerationEU (NGEU)) but has also obligated the Member States to introduce a new tax for the first time (known as the EU excess profits tax). This raises fundamental legal questions-particularly whether and to what extent the European Union has taxing powers, although proceeds of the excess profits tax are not part of the EU budget.

title: Data-Driven Triple Buffering for Resilient Supply Chains: Navigating Unspecified Correlations among Demand and Supply Uncertainties
affiliations: Shandong University, Shandong University, Shandong University and Shandong University

detail.title: Data-Driven Triple Buffering for Resilient Supply Chains: Navigating Unspecified Correlations among Demand and Supply Uncertainties
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Effectively addressing supply and demand uncertainties has emerged as a critical concern in modern supply chain management. The "Triple Buffering Strategy" (TBS)-which integrates capacity reservation, supplier diversification, and safety stock-has been widely adopted by firms to enhance supply chain resilience. However, the practical implementation of TBS is often complicated by the limited observability and measurability of interdependencies among uncertainties. Methodology/results: This paper explicitly incorporates unspecified correlation structures among demand, supply, and their interactions by leveraging a unified distributionally robust optimization (DRO) approach. We develop and analyze three models: one under fully ambiguous correlation with known marginals, and two others with partial knowledge of linear and rank correlations, respectively. For the fully ambiguous case, we characterize the worst-case distributions and derive closed-form solutions by exploiting the supermodular structure of the cost function. For the partially specified cases, we provide equivalent linear programming reformulations to ensure computational tractability. Our results reveal that the underlying correlation structure exerts a profound impact on optimal safety stock levels, capacity reservations, and supplier selection, underscoring the necessity of accounting for correlation beyond traditional cost and reliability considerations. Managerial implications: We derive a shadow price analysis that yields managerial insights for prioritizing future data collection and structural learning regarding correlation. Extensive numerical experiments validate the effectiveness and robustness of our models, demonstrating that stronger correlations induce greater TBS investments, higher total costs, and more concentrated capacity allocations. These findings provide actionable guidance for managing correlation risk and designing resilient supply chain strategies in the face of uncertainty.

title: Technology Integration in Teaching: A Panacea in Achieving Active Learning Strategies
affiliations: University of Abuja

detail.title: Technology Integration in Teaching: A Panacea in Achieving Active Learning Strategies
detail.abstract: This paper critically examines technology integration as a purported panacea for implementing active learning strategies in education. While digital tools offer transformative potential, enhancing engagement, collaboration, inquiry, and authentic creation-significant limitations challenge this universal remedy. Infrastructure deficits (e.g., unreliable internet in rural settings), equity gaps, risks of passive consumption, and teacher competency gaps undermine technology's efficacy. Through the lens of the TPACK framework (Mishra & Koehler, 2006), the study argues that technology alone cannot guarantee active learning; instead, its power emerges only when strategically integrated by skilled educators who prioritize pedagogical goals over tools. The paper concludes that sustainable active learning requires balancing technology with human interaction, critical thinking, and context-sensitive design, positioning teachers, not tools as the true catalysts of educational transformation.

title: Designing Human-Centered Organizations: From Value Extraction to Cultural Contribution
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Designing Human-Centered Organizations: From Value Extraction to Cultural Contribution
detail.abstract:
Organizations across industries face mounting pressure from rapid technological change, ecological crises, and shifting social expectations. While many achieve financial success, they often do so at the expense of long-term resilience and cultural contribution. This paper introduces the concept of Human-Centered Organizations (HCOs) as a framework for moving beyond extractive models of value creation toward sustainable, systemic, and purpose-driven practices.

Drawing on insights from innovation ecosystems, design methodologies, and cultural studies, the HCO framework establishes six guiding principles: Purpose-Driven Value Creation, Holistic Stakeholder Stewardship, Intergenerational Responsibility, Ethical Design and Accountability, Empathetic and Adaptive Systems, and Ecological Regeneration. Together, these principles reframe technology not as an end in itself but as an enabler of human productivity and contribution.

The paper further integrates three applied frameworks developed by the author — SP3 (Strength–People–Problem–Product), ABC (Appeal–Benefit–Convenience), and Insights Weaver — to operationalize human-centered innovation across startups, SMEs, and corporates. By embedding empathy, culture, and sustainability into organizational design, Human-Centered Organizations offer a pathway to aligning financial performance with enduring human and ecological value.

title: The National Anthem and Social Cohesion in Colombia (1887-2025) National Anthem and Social Cohesion
affiliations: EDUKIVOTOS

detail.title: The National Anthem and Social Cohesion in Colombia (1887-2025) National Anthem and Social Cohesion
detail.abstract: This academic article analyzes the symbolic value of the chorus of the Colombian National Anthem-"Oh unfading glory, oh immortal joy, in furrows of sorrow, goodness already germinates"-as a central element in the construction of identity and social cohesion. From a sociological perspective based on the theory of Émile Durkheim and cultural transmission approaches, the article examines how this patriotic expression has endured over generations, shaping collective imaginations and influencing the legitimacy of public administration. The article explores the relationship between national symbols, governability, and a sense of belonging in a country plagued by conflicts and territorial transformations.

reference: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-118
title: Superstar Firms through the Generations
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, University of Notre Dame - Department of Economics, London Business School and Kiel Institute for the World Economy

detail.title: Superstar Firms through the Generations

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-118
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We present new facts about the largest American companies over the past century. In manufacturing, top firms in the 1910s, 1950s, and 2010s predominantly date back to around 1900. Even as this special generation persists, turnover among top firms has been substantial. In contrast, in retail and wholesale, we do not observe a special generation among top firms. We show in a model of firm dynamics that a special generation can arise from an industrial revolution, through the adoption of a scalable technology and learning-by-doing. Top firm turnover is matched by standard idiosyncratic productivity shocks. Time-varying market size growth rates or entry costs are not sufficient to explain the facts. Among retailers and wholesalers, learning appears absent, so a special generation would be harder to sustain. Our results highlight the potential for lasting nonstationarity among the dynamics of top firms, which can result from the long echoes of technological change.

title: Analysis of Crash Contributing Factors in Worker-Involved Crashes in Ohio Work Zones: A Topic Modeling Approach
affiliations: University of Cincinnati and University of Cincinnati

detail.title: Analysis of Crash Contributing Factors in Worker-Involved Crashes in Ohio Work Zones: A Topic Modeling Approach
detail.abstract: Nationwide, work zone-related crashes have shown a rising trend since 2013. In 2022 alone, there were 37,701 injuries in work zones, with 891 fatalities - an increase from 845 in 2019 and 863 in 2020. A similar pattern is evident in Ohio, which recorded 29,000 work zone crashes between 2019 and 2024. This study seeks to uncover contributing factors to worker-involved crashes in work zones by analyzing unstructured crash narratives using various text mining techniques: word cloud visualization, Yet Another Keyword Extractor (YAKE), Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), and Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers for Topic Modeling (BERTopic). Another objective is to compare LDA and BERTopic in their ability to extract coherent and distinct topics from crash narratives. The word cloud emphasized frequent mentions of vehicle-worker interactions and traffic control features. YAKE identified “stop sign” as a key term, suggesting issues with temporary traffic control. LDA’s inter-topic distance map showed overlapping themes, indicating semantic similarity. In contrast, BERTopic generated eight well-separated topics, highlighting its strength in distinguishing detailed crash contexts. LDA modeling identified six key topics, including interstate incidents, flagger operations, intersection-related crashes, marked zone areas, worker-vehicle interactions, and documentation aspects. BERTopic provided greater detail, distinguishing eight distinct topics such as signage-related crashes, traffic direction issues, and utility-related incidents. These findings highlight the need for improved traffic control measures and policy revisions to protect workers. This research offers a foundation for targeted safety interventions based on specific crash scenarios derived from narrative analysis, enhancing the operation of safer work zones.

title: Is Beta Busted?
affiliations: , , University of Technology Sydney and University of Technology Sydney (UTS) - School of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Is Beta Busted?
detail.abstract: The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) is one of the most widely used tools in finance, linking expected returns to market risk. Yet the way beta is typically estimated can produce misleading results. We show that using standard market indexes as proxies introduces a systematic bias and propose a measure of its severity, the Beta Mismatch Error. Analysing 30 years of U.S. equity data, we find that OLS betas understate theoretical betas by around 50% on average. Extending to portfolios, we show that the size and value premiums largely reflect this mismatch, casting doubt on many findings based on CAPM estimates.

title: Which is Better: Democracy, Monarchy, or Other Types of Government? A Comparative Study of Governance Models Across History and Nations
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Which is Better: Democracy, Monarchy, or Other Types of Government? A Comparative Study of Governance Models Across History and Nations
detail.abstract: The question of which form of government best serves society-democracy, monarchy, or alternative systems such as authoritarianism, socialism, or theocracy-remains one of the most enduring debates in political philosophy and practice. At the same time, democracy is often heralded as the pinnacle of governance in the modern world; however, history and contemporary case studies reveal that no single model guarantees prosperity, stability, or justice in all contexts. This paper examines the origins, philosophical underpinnings, and historical evolution of major governance systems, beginning with classical monarchy and its variants, progressing through the rise of democracy, and extending to authoritarian, socialist, and hybrid regimes. Using comparative case studies-including the economic modernization of constitutional monarchies like the United Kingdom, the democratic resilience of India, the authoritarian stability of China, and the hybrid theocratic-monarchic structure of Saudi Arabia-this research evaluates governance models through the lenses of social development, political stability, and economic performance. The analysis highlights the trade-offs inherent in each system: democracy's inclusivity versus inefficiency, monarchy's continuity versus lack of accountability, authoritarianism's efficiency versus repression, and socialism's equality versus rigidity. Ultimately, this paper argues that no system is universally "best"; rather, effectiveness depends on historical, cultural, and socioeconomic contexts. By situating governance within both theory and practice, the paper contributes to the broader debate on how nations can adapt political systems to achieve sustainable progress in the 21st century. This research provides a comprehensive analysis of twenty-three types of governance systems spanning historical, contemporary, and niche models, including democracy, monarchy, technocracy, autocracy, anarchism, and transitional governments. Each system is examined in depth, covering historical origins, core features, political structures, economic and social implications, and illustrative case studies. The study further provides a comparative analysis to evaluate the effectiveness, strengths, weaknesses, and situational suitability of these systems, emphasizing lessons for modern governance. By integrating historical context with contemporary relevance, this research offers a holistic guide for understanding how diverse governance structures shape societal outcomes, inform policy-making, and influence development trajectories.

title: Magnetic Fluctuations and Neutral Current Features: From the 21-cm Hydrogen Line to Neurobiological Mechanisms
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin

detail.title: Magnetic Fluctuations and Neutral Current Features: From the 21-cm Hydrogen Line to Neurobiological Mechanisms
detail.abstract:
This study explores the potential for a fundamental connection between quantum phenomena at the cosmic scale and neurobiological processes, based on the underlying physical mechanisms of hydrogen 21-cm emission in the interstellar medium. We propose a unified theoretical framework linking the hyperfine transitions responsible for this cosmic emission to potential quantum processes in neuronal tissue.

The analysis draws upon an extension of Weinberg angular parameters and experimental measurements of neutral currents obtained at CERN, revealing that these currents can be up to ten times stronger than primary currents in atomic nuclei. We present computational calculations for various atomic species (hydrogen, helium, lithium) and develop a complex mathematical formalism to describe neutral current interactions in biological systems.

A crucial distinction emerges between these two quantum environments: in the interstellar medium, the massive bosons responsible for quantum coordination exhibit spin states of ±2 or 0, consistent with graviton-like particles and scalar field interactions, as demonstrated by our 4D superstring formulations (dE ≈ 125.57 GeV for spin-2 bosons). In contrast, in the neuronal environment, the mediating massive bosons are virtual W bosons of variable masses M_W-k, possessing spin ±1 and charges proportional to their masses, derived from the modified Weinberg angle θ_W-k where sin²θ_W-k = ±Ln(P)/(π + 4k3²π³/(Ln(P))²), with M_W ≈ 79.48 GeV.

The neuronal environment, rich in magnetically active ions (K⁺, Ca²⁺) and containing approximately 50 million hydrogen atoms per neuron, could theoretically support quantum magnetic resonance phenomena analogous to those observed in interstellar space. The endogenous electromagnetic fields generated by neuronal activity (10⁻¹⁵ to 10⁻¹² Tesla) could modulate nuclear spin states via electromagnetic coupling mediated by these ±1 spin massive bosons.

We examine glutamatergic and GABAergic neurotransmission mechanisms from the perspective of quantum coordination, proposing that glutamate-mediated excitation may promote coordinated spin states, while GABAergic inhibition may promote quantum decoherence. A computational algorithm adapted from particle physics is presented to detect signatures of neutral currents in biological systems.

The critical analysis acknowledges major physical constraints, notably the challenge posed by body temperature (26 meV) compared to the hyperfine transition energy (5.9 μeV), and decoherence timescales (femtoseconds to picoseconds) compared to neuronal processes (milliseconds). Nevertheless, quantum protection mechanisms analogous to those found in photosynthesis may preserve transient coherences in highly organized molecular structures.

Experimental implications include the use of high-resolution NMR spectroscopy, quantum magnetoencephalography, and tailored quantum correlation experiments in neurons. If confirmed, these phenomena could revolutionize our understanding of neural information processing, synaptic plasticity, and potentially contribute to quantum theories of consciousness.

This research proposes a bold conceptual bridge between astrophysics and neurobiology, suggesting that fundamental quantum principles may operate across radically different scales and environments—from interstellar space to biological neural networks—distinguished primarily by the spin characteristics of their respective mediating particles.

title: Gender and Tax Scholarship as Critical Method
affiliations: Pace University - School of Law

detail.title: Gender and Tax Scholarship as Critical Method
detail.abstract:
This Essay introduces the Pittsburgh Tax Review's issue featuring scholarship from the American Tax Policy Institute's October, 2024 symposium, "It's a Man's World: Revealing and Addressing Hidden Gender Bias in Tax Law and Policy." In reading the symposium papers together, this Essay advances a central claim: gender-aware tax analysis is not merely a topic but a method. Part I situates contemporary work within five decades of scholarship, tracing a shift from identifying overt statutory bias to interrogating how ostensibly neutral rules produce gendered and racialized outcomes. Part II maps the symposium's six panels that deployed diverse methods-doctrinal excavation, empirical measurement, comparative and constitutional analysis, and intersectional critique-to examine marriage and filing status, the production of legislative "evidence," care work and refundable credits, retirement and wealth-building, employment incentives and incarceration's collateral tax harms, and the tension between formal neutrality and measured effects. Part III looks forward, outlining research agendas on intersectional race-gender questions; immigrants and the tax state; transgender and nonbinary taxpayers; queer families; wealth transfers and trusts; capital gains and gendered asset patterns; entrepreneurship; exempt organizations; reproductive justice; and digital and algorithmic taxation. 

Across these contributions, the Essay identifies a common move in gender and tax scholarship to test neutrality empirically, read design choices against distributional facts, and center lived experience in policy architecture. The collective result is work that takes the form of both diagnosis and blueprint, offering tools for exposing hidden hierarchies in tax and for building systems that more accurately recognize work, caregiving, and diverse household forms.
